speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Last October, I filed a petition signed by my constituents with the Clerk of the House, as prescribed by the Standing Orders. A month later, two other ministers did the same.
In an article in La Presse, an employee of the House of Commons was quoted indirectly as saying that filing a petition directly with the Clerk instead of presenting it in the House might indicate that we disagreed with the position defended by the petitioners. The same employee also said there was nothing to compel us to act as messengers for groups with whose views we disagreed. For instance, a member opposed to abortion would probably not table a petition in favour of abortion.
Mr. Speaker, these comments are inaccurate. As you know, Canadian citizens have always had the right to petition the Crown and Parliament for redress of what might have been perceived as a grievance. I quote Beauchesne's, our authority on parliamentary procedure:
Although the House of Commons is a representative institution, it only considers questions submitted by its elected Members. Therefore the ordinary citizen has no right to appear personally before the House of Commons. If he has a grievance, he may present a written petition through a Member within the conditions laid down in the Standing Orders of the House.
The only elected representative in the House who is excluded from the responsibility to present petitions
from his constituents is the Speaker, the reason being that he might be called upon to rule on the irregularity of petitions.
Beauchesne's tells us in citation 689 that when the Speaker's constituents ask him to present a petition in the House of Commons on their behalf:
-he must avail himself of the services of another Member.
Beauchesne's indicates no other exceptions to the rule, whatever the responsibilities of the member, minister, backbencher, or Leader of the Opposition. It is his duty, as an elected representative, to present the petitions of his constituents. It is a duty, not a choice.
The personal beliefs of the member have no connection either with the principle or the practice. If a petition is duly certified by the clerk and signed by the member, it may, pursuant to the Standing Orders, be presented in the House during routine proceedings or filed directly with the clerk. In either case, the presentation is recorded in the Votes and Proceedings.
I and other members presented these petitions to discharge our duties to our constituents, whether or not we agreed with the content and irrespective of what is said when presenting petitions under Routine Proceedings or when filing them "by the backdoor" with the clerk of the House.
Mr. Speaker, an article in this morning's La Presse quotes the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier):
It shows lack of courage on the part of these ministers to table
petitions in the House by the back door, without commenting
publicly.
Mr. Speaker, Standing Order 36(7) allows no debate when a petition is presented. The article in La Presse continues:
Mr. Gauthier still wonders whether there are links between these
ministers and APEC.
I reject the suggestion that a member shows lack of courage by choosing to submit a petition to the clerk of the House.

February 13, 1990
Privilege
In fact, the quickest and most effective way is clearly to use a letter, instead of rising in the House. No one can question my courage on language rights. As Minister of State for Treasury Board, Deputy Leader of the Government in the House and Member of Parliament, I worked hard to pass Bill C-72. Many of my constituents criticize me for this active role. I am proud of it.
I support the linguistic duality of this country. I support it unequivocally. I do not belong to APEC. Furthermore, I deplore their opinions and everything they represent. However, as a member of Parliament, I must represent my constituents. Some members of APEC who live in my riding asked me to table their petition in the House. I did so and this gave the government an opportunity to answer them clearly and precisely.
I do not agree with APEC's opinions, but they have the right to have them presented in the House. And I have the right to decide how to do it without being accused of lacking courage.
I therefore ask my hon. friend to apologize to me and my colleagues.

Finally, in English, just in case I missed something. I want everyone to know something, and I mean this. WASPs have fought for minorities for centuries. We are going to continue that fight. We reject intolerance wherever we find it and we are always going to be there to preach tolerance and to protect the rights of minorities.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments following that statement, which I accept and feel should perhaps have been made some months ago. The whole matter raised by the minister is very important for the House and Canadians who respect not only our Constitution but also this country's official languages. I recognize that the minister has always been honest in dealing with this question and I also acknowledge his ability to rise in this House and maintain his position on official languages.
I must nevertheless tell the House that when a journalist calls us to ask, further to some items published in the press, why a minister did not comment or publicly table a petition, it is a known fact, Mr. Speaker, that in
this House-and I am not saying it, it was said long before I did-some hon. members, on fundamental issues affecting them, like official languages in my case or abortion for others-perhaps I should mention capital punishment or other similar subjects that are difficult for many members. These subjects require many of us to make painful decisions that are at times extremely difficult.
I think that the petition's authorship, even if it is signed by members of Parliament, is not the issue. We all know the Standing Orders. We know very well that petitions are usually a collective effort. In this case, the petitions had been organized by APEC, which is known as an extreme right-wing group on official languages and has long been dedicated to eliminating respect for both official languages, French and English, from this country, and making Canada unilingually English. I will fight that concept and I think that the minister will join us in that fight.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, whether we are talking about a petition by APEC or about the goods and services tax, or a petition for or against abortion, I don't think a minister who represents a cabinet that upholds cabinet solidarity, ought to or has the right to say: I am going to file this particular petition with the clerk as provided under Standing Order 35(6). I think the minister made his point, and perhaps when I said manque de courage, I was describing what I see as one of the problems some members have with rising in the House and saying: I condemn this policy aimed at killing the concept of official languages, but I table this petition as the member for a riding that contains certain groups which promote certain principles from which I wish to dissociate myself. It takes guts to do that, Mr. Speaker. I have done it before in the House, and the minister has done it often enough on other topics; today, he did it on the official languages issue. I respect him for that because he condemned, before this House, the APEC and what it represents. I am grateful for that, and I think all Canadians owe him a debt of gratitude for this important statement.
However, Mr. Speaker, with the kind of procedure we have in the House of Commons, it is sometimes difficult to keep up with the opinions expressed in petitions that are tabled through the clerk. When a petition is tabled openly in the House, everybody knows about it. It is in Hansard the next day, and everybody knows that peti-
February 13, 1990

tions were tabled. In fact, members on all sides of the House have tabled petitions on the official languages issue, APEC and Bill 178 in Quebec. However, I feel that the minister, as the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, did not entirely discharge his duties as a member of cabinet when he omitted to mention, although he was acting within the Standing Orders, that he was not at all associated with this petition. I agree the minister had the right to lay the petition on the Table of the House. However, I also feel that the minister should, from time to time, rise in the House and condemn this group that wants to destroy my country. I say this very seriously, Mr. Speaker. This group should be condemned by all members of this House. This is important to me.
To get back to the question of our parliamentary democracy, it is true that our system allows any group to table petitions in this House. It is a right that Canadians have had for many years. I don't contest that. However, a petition always contains a prayer, and that prayer reads as follows: "The petition of the undersigned, residents of Canada, who avail themselves of their ancient and undoubted right to present a grievance common to your petitioners, in the certain assurance that your honourable House will therefor provide a remedy".
Mr. Speaker, the petitioners, the people who signed the petition the minister tabled, have the certain assurance that the government or Parliament will provide a remedy for their problems. What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means abolishing official languages in this country. It means proclaiming this country to be a unilingual, English-speaking country Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to do that. And I don't think the minister is either. That is why I said that this roundabout, under-the-table way was not the right way, and I condemn the APEC. In concluding, I would like to repeat that if the minister felt hurt because I said that he lacked guts, he and his colleagues, I maintain this is not unparliamentary. Guts means rising in the House like he did today, and I thank him for it. It meant rising and condemning the group on whose behalf he tabled a petition in the House.
Privilege

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to add a few words to the comments made by my colleague, the Minister of Justice.

Mr. Speaker, the two articles in question have raised considerable concern for a number of us. The first appeared in La Presse on Saturday, the second appeared today.
The clear implication of those articles was that members of Parliament, in exercising their right and their responsibility to table petitions on behalf of their constituents, in the act of tabling those petitions, somehow indicate that they support the content of those petitions. Nothing could be further from the truth.
I think it is appropriate that we should use the vehicle of the question of privilege to, first of all, make it clear that those of us who have tabled these petitions in no way endorse their contents. I am not a supporter of APEC; I have not been a supporter of APEC in the past; I will not be a supporter of APEC in the future.
I would think that in 17 years in Parliament one develops a record which can be consulted by anyone who wishes to do so, in terms of the votes that one takes in Parliament, in terms of the positions that one takes in one's constituency and across the country. I think that, in the course of those seventeen and a half years that I have been privileged to serve in Parliament, I have developed some reputation for a belief in the preservation of rights across Canada, the belief that we should all fight against intolerance in whatever form, and the belief, as well, that all Canadians are entitled to the right of freedom of speech.
My practice, during the years in which I have served as a member of Parliament, has been to table petitions in the House of Commons which are presented by my constituents with the request that they be passed on to Parliament. I fully concede this fact up front; nothing in the rules requires that a member of Parliament discharge that moral responsibility anymore than anything in the rules requires that a member of Parliament vote in this place, or that a member of Parliament speak in debate,

February 13, 1990
Privilege
or that a member of Parliament discharge the many other responsibilities that he or she has. One of the most basic and fundamental rights for which people have fought and died is the right of freedom of speech. And the right to petition Parliament is a direct extension of the right of freedom of speech.
I do not believe that any of us has to say that we endorse everything that is said whenever someone exercises his or her freedom of speech. But, I think everyone in this House must surely accept the principle of freedom of speech as being sacrosanct. The principle of the right of citizens of this country to petition the Parliament of Canada must also be sacrosanct.
In the article in La Presse the journalist takes a good deal of time speculating as to whether those members of Parliament who table petitions support the contents of the petitions. The reporter had lots of time for doing that. What he did not have time to do was to bother to ask any of the members of Parliament in question what their position was.
I received no telephone call from that journalist before he wrote his article. Had he called, had he asked whether I supported APEC's petition, the answer would have been unequivocally "no". But, the journalist did not take the trouble to bother to find out. Instead, he simply speculated.
In the Saturday article there was a disturbing, unattributed quotation referring to fonctionnaire de la Chambre des communes, saying that members of Parliament typically would not table petitions with which they disagree. The individual who is alleged to have made that quote is not identified and I do not think any purpose is served by our trying to search him or her out. But, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appropriate for you-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt, but the hon. member referred to an apparently unidentified functionary of this place. I just want to tell the House that that person has not been identified and that person may not exist.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Finally, I would make two points with regard to the practice that is followed here. The first is that had the journalist in question bothered to check the record he would have been able to check other petitions that I have tabled during my time here in Parliament. He would have found, for example, that I have tabled petitions on abortion, an issue on which I hold very strong views and on which there is a bill before Parliament at the present time. I have tabled petitions which do not necessarily accord with my point of view on abortion.
I have attempted as well to table a petition in opposition to the goods and services tax. My support of the goods and services tax is well known. I am a minister of the Crown and my very membership in cabinet requires full support of all of the government's programs. Yet I sent to the clerk of petitions, as I believe is appropriate, a petition drawn up within my own constituency in opposition to the goods and services tax. It was rejected by the clerk of petitions because it was not drawn up in the right form. But the intention was there to allow my constituents to petition Parliament whenever they believe that they have a grievance that should be redressed.
The Minister of Justice and government House leader on behalf of the government responded, rejecting APEC's petition. That point should not be lost on anybody here-the government made a formal response to the APEC petitions rejecting the petitions. The La Presse article says that when the government House leader responded to it, he tabled the response in an equally discreet way, ostensibly one assumes to avoid anybody noticing that he had tabled a response. That is the only way in which a response can be given to petitions. It is the way in which a response is given daily to petitions. To suggest that there is something surreptitious or sneaky about tabling a response to petitions, which is the only way in which it can be done is simply a perversion of the facts.

Mr. Speaker, I detest intolerance in whatever form it comes. I have no affiliation and will have no affiliation with a movement that promotes intolerance and fear.
Privilege
That is my policy in French and it is my policy in English. It is the responsibility of every member of Parliament. As long as I am privileged to serve in this place, my policy will be to promote tolerance and understanding and not fear and intolerance. As long as I serve in this Parliament, my goal as well will be to ensure that the rights of freedom of speech of all Canadians are fully respected.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to put a few points on the record today with respect to the issue to which my colleagues the Ministers of Justice and National Health and Welfare have referred. The point that has to be mentioned here is that one has as much credibility in this House and in the country with respect to national leadership as the integrity with which one's words are taken and respected on both sides of the House.
We have partisan differences in this House, that is what this place is all about. On the other hand, there is always a deep understanding, which I have always appreciated in the 17 plus years that I have been here, that we respect the manner in which members deal with tough and difficult public issues and also their attempts to forge national unity.
Having said that, I want to make a couple of points. I will not repeat the legal arguments that my House Leader put before the House. I think those are quite clear. We understand them also from the House rules.
Second, we all recognize that since the earliest days of Parliament, going back to King John, the people had the right to petition the King, or as our modem expression is, the Parliament, and in our case the Parliament of Canada. That is my responsibility as a member of Parliament.
Having said that, and as the Minister of National Health and Welfare also pointed out, in fact, there have been petitions presented to me on the pro-choice side of the abortion question. I do not think I have to convince anybody in this House of my position on that issue, that being pro-life. But I had a responsibility in respect of the people in my riding, who do not universally hold the view I have on that subject, to present the petition.

February 13, 1990
Privilege
I want to go back just a bit to the time, Mr. Speaker, when you and I came into this House in 1972. In 1972, we had a minority. There was a difference of two seats in 1972. There was a resolution on reaffirmation of the Official Languages Act of 1969. I know the House Leader of the Liberal Party will recall that period. Those were periods of fairly difficult tension in respect to language. I remember the then Minister of Transport, the late hon. Jean Marchand, making a very impassioned speech from his seat in regard to the need for parties from both sides of the House to always keep in mind that our single responsibility, regardless of our partisan differences, was the unity of the country. That was a speech that obviously left an impression on a very young member of Parliament over all these years.
There was a vote in this House at that time on a resolution. If memory serves correctly, there were eight members from my party, from my province in this House. It was the only province from which the majority of members from one party, from one province, voted against the resolution. I voted for that resolution in 1973.
In fact, if I can be very personal for a moment, because of the minority situation at the time there was a member of my party whom I will not name, who later became a member of the Liberal party, who came into my riding to try to find a new member to contest the nomination, because of my support for bilingualism and for minority language rights in the province of Manitoba.
I say that simply because I think it is sometimes important to have the historical record in terms of continuity in respect of this issue. This is an issue which, I believe, goes beyond partisan differences.
I think we in this House all recognize that when we have petitions to present it creates a difficulty, not only for a member of Parliament but particularly for a cabinet minister, because you are both a member of Parliament and a cabinet minister. You have to respond to both roles and both functions.
With my staff in my office I looked at this petition and discussed whether I should present it in the House and make a statement and whether, in so doing, I would give this group in my riding the very publicity it craves, publicity which I was not going to give them. That was
one issue I had to deal with and it was for that reason the petition was presented that way.
I would like to make one last point, Mr. Speaker, or perhaps two if you allow me the time, because I know you take this issue very seriously. I was first made aware of this on Sunday through an article in La Presse and there is an article today in The Sun chain by Michel Gratton. He makes the statement:
They seem to think it was their democratic duty to their constituents.
That is to file petitions. Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is my democratic duty. Not only is it my duty, it is my responsibility even if I disagree with what is in the petition. More important, he says:
I fail to understand what pushing something you don't believe in has to do with a politician's duty.
My second point is that all of us have presented petitions in this House signed by constituents, with which petitions we fundamentally disagree.
As a matter of fact, there seems to be a contradiction there. We don't elect fax machines or mailmen. We like to believe we elect people who stand for something and are not mere vehicles for what any extremist pressure group wants them to do.
We also do not elect writers, we do not elect editorial writers, we do not elect people who can get on television or, for that matter, who have licences from the CRTC. We have public responsibility through that licensing process. We have another responsibility as members of Parliament to present the views of our constituents no matter how wrong we believe those views are.
I would like to take just another moment. I went to my records this morning because I wanted to see whether I had been true to the words I was going to use in the House of Commons. I have a letter dated November 24, 1989, which is signed by my special assistant in the riding that was addressed to the people who had demanded that I make a public statement in the tabling of this petition. I am willing to table these letters. I have as well the record of the House of Commons which, of course, everyone can read. More important, there is a letter dated October 5, 1989, and, because this matter has become public, I will do something that I do not do very often. I will make public a letter between a member of Parliament, a cabinet minister, and a constituent.
February 13, 1990

It is addressed to Mr. and Mrs. Tom Joyce, R. R. 1, Steinbach, Manitoba, ROA 2A0. In fact, the irony of this thing is that while that is an address in my home town the community that they live close to is a place called Giroux in the rural municipality of Ste-Anne-des-Chenes. That may gives members of this House a little glimpse of what we all face in our own constituencies.
I will not go into detail. He and she go into the matter of the CF-18 and the CF-5. I know members of the House know about that. They write about VIA Rail. I would like to read selective paragraphs only for the purpose of this debate and if people want to see this letter they can do that, even with the conditions I made earlier. I said this:
VIA Rail is a prime example of Quebec not being favoured when hard decisions must be made. There will be 227 people laid off in Manitoba because of VIA cuts. The province of Quebec will lose 1,000 jobs with 631 lay-offs in Montreal alone.
Then it goes into the Manitoba issue and the last part of the petition:
In your letter you accuse the government of not only giving lip service to the issue of minority rights but specifically in Quebec. The Prime Minister has objected to Bill 178 in terms as strong or stronger than Alberta and Saskatchewan and passed legislation affecting francophone rights in those provinces. In your letter you called for less talk and more positive action. In my view one positive step that can be taken on a personal level is learning more about the situation on minorities and the history of francophone rights in Canada. This would lead to greater understanding and reduced linguistic tensions. As you are not satisfied with the position of the Government of Canada I am asking for your suggestions as to what positive action should be taken. What would you like to see done? When answering this question keep in mind two key points: One, I do not consider a boycott of Quebec products to be positive. Traditionally the federal government does not punish provinces, fiscally, financially or legally, for passing legal legislation the government does not support. Two, the actions of Quebec, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, while regrettable, were legal. The Canadian constitution has a notwithstanding clause that allows provinces to override the Charter of Rights when deemed necessary in the provinces view.
In conclusion the federal government continues to oppose the violation of minority rights everywhere in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot put it any clearer in the House today than I did in that letter of October last.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to intervene briefly in this matter. I want the House and all of Canada to know that this matter goes beyond the case that has caught the attention of the House and
Privilege
extends to the manner and circumstances in which petitions are presented to the House of Commons.
I want, first, to draw your attention to an incident that took place in the House last Friday, February 9, 1990, and involved the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca and the member for Calgary Southwest. I am sorry, in view of the discussion today, that I did not rise on a point of order at that time. As became apparent as reported at page 8144 of the official report, Hansard, the exchange speaks for itself, but it bears repeating.
The member for Juan de Fuca said, and it was later apparent that he meant the member for Calgary Southwest:
You cannot even accept the fact that some people who wear turbans
are Canadians. I find that disgraceful. I will not even deal with that.
The member for Calgary Southwest denied emphatically that she had ever indicated that that was her view. It appeared then that the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca was relying on a petition that the member for Calgary Southwest had presented on another occasion, and an argument ensued about presenting petitions.
Once more, we are the author of our own misfortune in the House of Commons. We have enacted and passed rules that are difficult to interpret, and I can understand why the media has some difficulty.
Members of Parliament have been presented with a form emanating, I understand, from the clerk of petitions. That form states very clearly in the notations that a member of Parliament cannot be compelled to present a petition. The form further notes that the fact that a member presents a petition does not imply that he or she endorses its contents. I think any member who reads that form is entitled to rely on that statement but, notwithstanding, that statement is contained in a form issued by the clerk of petitions of this House of Commons.
The rules of the House state, and I refer to Standing Order 36(3):
Members presenting petitions shall be answerable that they do not
contain impertinent or improper matter.

February 13, 1990
Privilege
A member is required to endorse his or her name on a petition. So, we create a confusion as to what is the status of a member when presenting a petition. On the one hand, there is no endorsement of the contents. On the other hand, it is said in the Standing Orders of the House that a member is responsible for improper matter in a petition.
I think we have created this difficulty, because the nature of a petition and the right to petition belongs to the petitioner, the Canadian subject, the citizen. The member of Parliament is only the instrument for the presentation of the petition. I do not see how any common sense can be made of requiring a member to endorse the contents of a petition. It takes away from the right of Canadians to petition the House of Commons if you make it a condition of that presentation that the member must, somehow, connect himself or herself to the contents of the petition by way of endorsement or otherwise.
I hope you will take this matter carefully under advisement, review the form that has been provided by the clerk of petitions, and review Standing Order 36 and particularly subsection (3) in the context not only of the case that is presented today but the context of the allegations made by the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. And I am sure other members have made similar allegations.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, in considering the rules and the forms that have been presented to us that you will come down on the side of the citizen and say that there does exist an inherent right of all Canadians to petition Parliament and that the role of the member of Parliament should simply be that of presenting a petition without comment, endorsement or otherwise.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take only a few minutes to add a few words on the very important point that was raised this morning.
First, Mr. Speaker, I guess you will be called upon to decide whether the issue should be referred to the parliamentary committee in order to determine whether changing our Standing Orders would be necessary in order to clarify what, in fact, the duty of the member is in such instances.
Our rules at the present time are somewhat vague in that regard. Perhaps that is the strength of the rule that
exists. It allows members of Parliament to make a decision according to his or her own conscience whether or not they will present a petition with which they agree, present a petition with which they disagree and believe in their own conscience it is their duty to do so, or feel so strongly opposed to the subject matter in question as to refuse to present the petition altogether.
I suppose each and every one of us has to make those kinds of decisions all day long when we are defending constituents, be they constituents with an unemployment insurance problem or any other kind of problem that we are called upon to rectify from time to time for those who have sent us here on their behalf.
In similar manner, rules are designed, I would argue, to reflect that in regard to petitions. In other words, we can make those kinds of decisions of conscience to which I was referring a while ago.
Our petition form, Mr. Speaker, which our rules provide for us, refers to the ancient and undoubted right to petition Parliament. Clearly, what is insinuated here is if a person has a right to petition Parliament, obviously Parliament has an obligation to receive the petition, and in order for Parliament to have that obligation to receive it, I think one can safely deduce that the parliamentarian in question has the same duty to present the petition in question.
I have in the past presented petitions with which I disagreed. In the Ontario legislature, where I had the honour and privilege of serving prior to coming to this House, I have upon occasion stated publicly while presenting a petition, albeit briefly and without presenting argument, that I was presenting a petition signed by so many constituents with whom I disagreed, and so on, and described the petition. I did not make an argument as to why I disagreed with it but merely stated so in one or two words. The point is that I felt this was a happy medium between my fulfilling my duty as a member of Parliament on the one hand and, of course, making it quite clear that I did not necessarily endorse the petition that I was presenting.
That, I believe, is the issue before us today; whether or not it is our duty to present petitions. I do not suppose we will solve that situation today, but I would argue that perhaps we should not, perhaps that issue should be left to the conscience of individual members.
February 13, 1990

I would argue, though, that all members of the House should reflect upon whether or not it would be appropriate for them to state briefly, and in the manner that I have indicated before, at the time they are presenting petitions, that they do not agree with the petition if they feel that the disagreement is so profound that they must say so. Of course, they would do that without presenting argument in order not to deviate otherwise from the rules at our disposal.
The fact that Mr. Speaker himself cannot present a petition but can ask a colleague to do so, I believe, is a demonstration of the fact that if the Speaker is presented with a petition the rules indicate that it would be Mr. Speaker's role to ensure that the petition is presented. By extension, it would be, I believe, the duty of the parliamentarian who was requested by Mr. Speaker to do so himself or herself after having received that request from the Speaker. That is a further illustration of the fact that the parliamentarian does not necessarily indicate support for the petitions.
In regard to presenting petitions, perhaps our role, to a degree, is that of a messenger. It is said that we should not shoot the messenger because the messenger does not necessarily agree with the message that he or she carries. Perhaps this is an example of that.
However, because of our duty of leadership in this House, as well as our duty as representatives, I think it would be important if we were provided with some mechanism by which we could, without debate, when we disagree with an issue to such a point that we feel it is in our interests, in the interests of this House and that of our country, I would argue in the present case, make that case very briefly.
Perhaps the other lesson to be learned from all of this is that in an issue as fundamental as this one we all, collectively and individually, should use every occasion to indicate our support for the linguistic duality and the national unity of our country. It has been said that all that is needed for evil to triumph is for good people to do nothing.
I am not suggesting that the three cabinet ministers in question failed to do something which they should have known to do. Rather, sometimes as parliamentarians we seem to take things for granted such as the recognition of that linguistic duality and other privileges and rights
Privilege
that we enjoy as citizens. Maybe we should never take those privileges and rights for granted.
I am not sure whether all of this constitutes a question of privilege but I want to leave you with one last remark. Perhaps I could get the attention of the three ministers in question. There may be something in the article signed by Mr. Michel Gratton that has been missed in all of this. The last line of the article reads:
Well, all I have to say to this timorous trio is: Next time, if you really
want to hide, put some hoods on.
I feel that that is a very offensive comment and if anything in this constitutes a question of privilege, that is probably the statement, more than anything else that has been said this morning.
This is not attributed to anyone else. I am saying that references which I interpret to be to the Ku Klux Klan are very offensive to all of us. Notwithstanding partisan disagreements which we may have, I invite colleagues to think about that particular statement in the article in question because I think it is more offensive than anything else that has been discussed in this debate.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words on this very important issue. I have asked myself why we have taken nearly an hour of time this morning to reflect on this issue. I think it is important. I have listened with interest to all the interventions and I find myself agreeing with most of the comments made today.
I must say that one of the times that I feel best in this House is when we are discussing, either in this way or in some other way, what this country is all about, the need for all of us to work together to preserve the unity that we know can exist in our country and to speak out against forces that cause rifts regionally or between cultures and peoples and, in this case of course, linguistic minorities.
I am pleased to listen to the elevated debate taking place today on this point of privilege. I am pleased that you have allowed us to go on at some length on this most important matter. That is the reason we have gone on. I do not have much to add to the points made by my distinguished colleagues other than to say that when I read both of those articles over the last few days, I was disgusted with the tone. I reflected back, when I read the articles, on others in the House who have raised similar petitions, exact petitions in terms of the source. I suppose the fact that most people dissociated themselves

February 13, 1990
Routine Proceedings
with the theme of the petitions rescued them from this particular journalist's wrath.
We all recognize that we can file petitions which indeed we have a right to do, and which the ministers referred to in the article did. Or we have the right to present petitions and most often petitioners from my constituency ask me to present their petitions in the House of Commons. Most of the time I do that enthusiastically because I agree with the thrust of the petition. However on occasion I have not. At that time I have simply dissociated myself with the point or points being raised in the petition and went on to present it. Surely, as a previous minister indicated, one of the most fundamental rights of a citizen in our country is to have his or her view presented on the floor of the House of Commons when the request is made to the member of Parliament.
Earlier some comments were made in then House by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. If we are to pursue I would certainly ask that we do it when the hon. member is in his place, to allow him to respond. I was here and I do not believe that what the hon. member indicated took place actually took place at all. However, that is for another time.
I simply would like to conclude by saying that we must uphold the right of all citizens to present petitions through their members of Parliament in the House of Commons but also to guard against using these times, when we are dealing with such sensitive issues in terms of nation building, to allow our partisan instincts to come to the fore. I have deep concerns over the points being raised by my hon. friend, the government House leader, on this case. However I suspect that you have heard enough now, Mr. Speaker, to make a ruling as to whether or not this is a question of privilege.
I would simply like to add that we have taken an hour of the time of an opposition day. I would like to think that we can at least add this hour to the end of the day. This is an extraordinary question of privilege and I would ask that at some later time that point be considered.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
First, I am in total agreement with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis), the other minister, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and other members that the subject considered today is very important. It is not only important for the procedure of this place; it is also very important for our country's unity. Again this morning, we heard statements about this House and against some attitudes that we have today and we also had in the past from some citizens in our country.
I greatly regret the situation, but it is clear that this House is unanimously against such statements and there is consensus to take the leadership positions required for our country to continue, to maintain Canadian unity, an attitude, a place where the rights of all Canadians are respected.

Having said that, I am going to take under advisement some of the issues that are raised here. I am mindful of the request of the hon. member for Kamloops that I consider carefully the matter raised by the hon. member for Halifax West. I will do that.
I want also to note, in addition to what I have said about the declarations on both sides of this House, that our colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, has today saluted the courage and the forthrightness of the ministers who were the subject of these articles.
I am concerned about the articles, and I am going to be very careful before I return to the House with some comments which will probably have to be made. I will try to do everything I can to put them in a way which will be helpful to the challenges that we face in trying to keep this country together. I thank hon. members for their interventions.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a challenge to the effectiveness of certain land withdrawals in the Yukon which could seriously undermine the government's ability to manage Yukon lands.
Consequently I am announcing today that the government is bringing forward legislation to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act and the Yukon Placer Mining Act. It will firmly establish the Crown's right to prohibit disposition of mineral rights on Yukon lands which are required for a purpose that the government believes to be in the public interest.
This legislation, if passed by Parliament, will be retroactive to this day. The government's action will assure that withdrawn lands, including lands identified as being of interest to Yukon Indians, will not be open for location of new mining claims.
I am making this announcement to ensure that the mining industry clearly knows which areas are open for staking and exploration.
The mining recorders in the Yukon maintain records of the areas withdrawn from disposition. Persons who intend to stake mining claims in the Yukon should first contact the mining recorders to determine the status of the lands. I am directing the mining recorders to refuse any application for claim which has been located in an area withdrawn from disposition.
These changes will deal only with withdrawal of lands. There is an urgency to make these technical changes in order to confirm the government's authority to manage Crown lands in the Yukon. This however will not preclude making other changes which have been identified by various interest groups and acknowledged in the northern mineral policy. It is certainly not my intention to introduce significant policy changes without full consultation with all interested parties.
Routine Proceedings
In addition, I wish to make clear that the statements I am making today do not affect the current action in the Federal Court of Canada, namely, Halferdahl v. M. A. Fish in his capacity as the mining recorder, et al.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nearly three decades have passed since the tragedy of thalidomide claimed more than 8,000 victims around the world. In Canada, a special commitment was made to thalidomide victims by the government of the day. Much was done by both federal and provincial governments to help meet their needs.
The thalidomide victims have faced a courageous struggle since birth, trying to adapt to and overcome disabling birth defects. Some cannot work or have problems finding jobs. All are reaching an age when they must establish their independence from parents who are growing older. They need extra funds to help pay for special transportation, housing or other needs not covered by provincial assistance programs.
At the time the tragedy occurred, two separate inquiries, a special parliamentary committee and a committee of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons, provided recommendations that enabled the government to assist these people and to prevent further such tragedies. This was on the basis of compassion or understanding and not liability. The commitment made by the minister of the day was unique. No similar commitment had ever been made to other groups.

Thalidomide victims have to face great challenges and they do so very courageously. For me and my colleagues in Cabinet, there is no doubt that we must help them improve their quality of life and plan their future.

I am pleased to announce today that the Government of Canada will fulfill its commitment made to the thalidomide victims in 1963 by providing a total of $7.5 million to an estimated 75 to 100 people living in Canada who were affected.

The $7.5 million will be divided equally among those who suffered injuries due to Kevadon or TMmol, the forms of thalidomide prescribed to their mothers during
pregnancy. Payment will be made to each eligible recipient in two equal annual tax-free instalments. Those concerned will have one year starting today to prove their eligibility.

I would like to assure everyone that the funding I am announcing today is over and above the settlements the victims received from the manufacturer of thalidomide and will not be taken from federal-provincial programs which help these disabled Canadians.
Canadians are proud of our social programs. They are proud of the fact that we try to care for those who are less fortunate, and they see it as one of the elements which distinguishs us from other countries. I believe that by announcing extraordinary assistance for people who have faced a genuine hardship, this government is showing that it supports this tradition.

Mr. Speaker, I begin by congratulating Mr. Randy Warren as well as Cliff Chadderton of the War Amputations of Canada, as well as the gentlemen who headed the task force on thalidomide victims. These individuals and their organizations have exhibted over the years great enthusiasm, as well as providing hope to their members.
Today, what I think we see is a realization of that particular objective in that the Government of Canada has accepted in whole the principle of compensation for these particular victims.
I am sure that the minister would want to join with me in congratulating the organization and all those individuals who have worked with him over the years in order to arrive at this particular day in terms of accepting of the principle of compensation.
The amount of money which has been put forward, amounting to $7.5 million, has not been fully accepted by the thalidomide victims and their organization. The Minister is well aware of that. I believe, and I am sure the Minister would want to echo my sentiments, that this is certainly a good starting point in terms of further negotiations which will take place over the next number of months. I am sure if there are any ways in which things can be changed to better the victims and their plight in life that the minister would want to co-operate in

:

whatever that might be, for example, monthly payments as opposed to annual payments, or whatever.
This particular issue has been around for almost three decades. It is ironic that last February 14 a report was tabled with the minister recommending compensation for these particular victims. I am happy to see that the Government of Canada has responded, not as quickly as I had hoped, but has responded favourably in terms of recognizing the principle of compensation.
I hope that it will proceed forward and meet with those representatives and meaningfully discuss ways to ensure that the compensation goes directly to the victims in a way in which they believe to be appropriate and responsible.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, in his very ably argued question of privilege yesterday, raised a matter which has been before this Parliament before. Because of the adjournment of the discussion which was sought and obtained yesterday by the hon. parliamentary secretary, I was able to review some of the precedents that I think are relevant to assist Your Honour in reaching a decision on this important matter.
It may be that we could obtain the agreement of the House on it. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary, when I have completed my remarks, will find unanimous agreement to treat this as a breach of privileges of the House and to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges, Procedure and Private Members' Business with a view to having it discussed and settled there.
The point raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre deals with the fact that a bill has been introduced in this House which purports to be retroactive in its application, but the government has proceeded
Routine Proceedings
to treat the bill as passed and has refused to pay out money it could pay out under the existing legislation, under the Railway Act, to persons who apply for this subsidy or payment for the shipment of grain to eastern ports.
A similar situation arose in 1971. Mr. Stanley Knowles, who was then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, raised a question of privilege on September 13, 1971 in relation to a government bill which dealt with the matter of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Wheat Board was doing the same thing that the government is currently doing with this legislation; that is to say, a bill had been introduced in Parliament that was to be retroactive in its effect, but the Wheat Board treated the bill as passed and was refusing to make the payments.
The hon. member as he then was raised this question of privilege and said, as reported on page 7737 of Hansard:
My question of privilege relates to the non-payment of moneys which it is specified in the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act are to be paid by the Minister of Finance to the Canadian Wheat Board; and, more particularly, the action of the government in telling this House that the reason it is not carrying out the provisions of the law is that it has a bill on the order paper.
I submit that anything which in a court would be regarded as contempt can be regarded as privilege in this House. I further suggest that when the government admits to Parliament that it is not carrying out the law and tells Parliament the reason it is not carrying out the law is that it has a bill on the order paper to rescind that law, a bill which has not yet been passed, then the rights and privileges of Parliament are being affronted.
On page 7738 he went on to state that the bill had not been passed and said:
One other point I cite in the list of facts is that Bill C-244 has not been passed and therefore authority to act on that basis has not been established by Parliament.
That is exactly the situation we are facing today in this House. He went on to state:
The point I am making is that the place for us to deal with a matter like this and what has been done to us is here on the floor of Parliament. What has been done to us is that we have been told that, although we have passed a law and although it is there and is clear, the government feels it does not have to carry it out because of this other provision, an unpassed bill which it has on the order paper.
What Mr. Knowles described was exactly the situation that we are faced with today. The Speaker on that question of privilege made a ruling. I will invite you later,

February 13, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Mr. Speaker, to consider that ruling. Tie ruled against Mr. Knowles' question of privilege, but I shall return to that later.
Subsequently, because of this outrageous conduct on the part of the then government, the hon. member for Calgary North sought and obtained leave to have an emergency debate on this issue.
If the Chair feels this is significant, I am quite prepared to bring an application for an emergency debate tomorrow to discuss this matter further, subject to what we hear today from the parliamentary secretary.
Clearly the complaint today is as outrageous as the complaint. I know that the Speaker would want to follow the ruling of the previous Speaker in this respect and permit an emergency debate should it be necessary. I hope it will not be.
Mr. Woolliams, the hon. member for Calgary North at the time, said, and I quote from page 7890 of Hansard for September 16, 1971:
This debate poses the rhetorical question: Is this institution of Parliament, which includes the House of Commons, the Senate and all the law-making processes, to be one that will be controlled by the executive?
That is the point of our question of privilege today.
That emergency debate revealed the most amazing speeches. I have found a veritable gold mine of assistance for Your Honour in it. Probably the most important statements were those by the now Minister of Agriculture who was then the hon. member for Vegre-ville. I gather he is still the hon. member for Vegreville, but he is now the Minister of Agriculture and Deputy Prime Minister, and a very distinguished member, one whom I know on procedural matters Your Honour would take as a great authority.
I would like to read from page 7902 of Hansard because I think his words are extremely helpful in considering this point today:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate we have a very basic and fundamental issue to consider. That issue is the deliberate and calculated failure of this government to carry out its administrative responsibility pursuant to Canadian law.
He went on to state:
If a question involving the administration of laws created by parliamentary democracy cannot be properly debated, it will be a
sad day for Canada, for Parliament and for the system of parliamentary democracy.
Never have I seen, and never did I expect to see, a government so blatantly and contemptuously refusing to carry out its administrative duty, a duty which is imposed by Canadian statute passed by Parliament, a law which remains in force and will continue to remain in force until Parliament in its wisdom sees fit to rescind it.
These words apply four-square to the situation we are faced with today. I know that if the Deputy Prime Minister were here now, he would stand up and agree with everything that he said in 1971.
That fact is so elementary that one could never have conceived that this situation could occur. It is a disgrace and a shame. After all, if governments cannot conform with the law, how in heaven's name can anyone else in society be expected to do so?
Imagine, the wisdom of Solomon uttered by the Deputy Prime Minister who went on to state:
How can society be expected to abide by laws if the government will not live up to them? This fact is so elementary, basic and fundamental that it is completely beyond my comprehension to understand the government's attitude.
Surely in light of those statements, the Minister of Agriculture who is really affected by this bill because it does deal with the shipment of grain and grain products to eastern Canada and clearly falls in part under his departmental jurisdiction would not want to retract those statements made in 1971.
I know that my colleague, the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader, has probably discussed this matter extensively with the Deputy Prime Minister. I think I know what he is going to propose, and I want to say that I quite agree with him.
The ruling of the Chair in 1971 suggested very strongly that this was not a question of privilege then. I say to Your Honour that times, I hope, have changed. Notwithstanding the very able and capable decision from, I believe it was, Mr. Speaker Lamoureux, and notwithstanding the great esteem in which he is held by all members and the authority that his decisions have, perhaps he erred on this occasion.
I would invite Your Honour to so find and in fact find that there is a question of privilege here. It may not be necessary because I know that the hon. parliamentary secretary, in his discussions with the Deputy Prime

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to my hon. friend with great care and I must say that I was almost persuaded by his rhetoric. It was very persuasive and a very well put argument. Unfortunately, once again the rhetoric is very distant and 180 degrees opposed to the facts. He did present an excellent argument. I thank him for that. It was very entertaining and very persuasive. Nevertheless, I know that the Speaker must look at the facts and not the rhetoric.
As I understand the argument of the hon. member from the NDP yesterday, he said that essentially it is unconstitutional for us to cease a subsidy before the appropriate legislation has received Royal Assent from the Governor General. In fact, what is happening in this case is that this particular bill is a direct result of budget measures. It has been done according to a very common practice used by this government and previous governments. It is nothing unusual.
In this particular case, the Minister of Finance announced the end of the at and east grain and flour subsidy when he tabled his budget paper on April 27, 1989. So it was part of the budget process. It was announced at that time. On June 16, 1989, Bill C-26 was introduced and read a first time.
What is really important here is what happened then. The House went on to approve the budget in principle. The House voted on it, made a decision on it, approved that announcement of the minister and what we have flowing out of it is the enabling legislation. That is very simple, very much a fact and not rhetoric. What we are dealing with in Bill C-26 is simply the legislation flowing out of that budgetary decision made by the House of Commons several months ago.
Once again I want to bring to the attention of the House that we have seen the demonstration we see so often in this House, that the hon. member representing the Liberal party has managed to stand on both sides of the equation, but of course at different times.
If we look back to a very good example of a similar piece of legislation, it would of course be the ruling of 1971 which the Speaker made at that time. However, even as recently as the budget debate of June 28, 1982, there was introduction of an act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada. It was acted upon,

February 13, 1990
Routine Proceedings
the budget was passed, and later on the legislation was passed.
Let's go back to the facts and not to the very amusing and entertaining rhetoric. The facts say very clearly that, as persuasive as the hon. member's arguments were, it is not a case of privilege. The actions taken on Bill C-26 are in keeping with the House of Commons practice and traditions, and I might say have been acted upon in the most proper fashion by this government, as is our usual standard.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF AT AND EAST PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to take up the time of my own party on our opposition day. I will be brief.
I remind you, Sir, of remarks I made yesterday on Bill C-26. With reference to the question of privilege raised by my colleague from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, I know the Chair will examine the precedents with care.
The Chair ruled against the question of privilege raised by the then member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Knowles in 1971, and subsequently the issue was taken to Federal Court. I was very closely and heavily involved with that. In the preliminary hearing before the Federal Court judge in Regina, the Deputy Minister of Justice made his pitch and the lawyer for four farmers who had a direct interest in the matter made his pitch. The judge, in the process of setting a trial date said to the government representative, the lawyer for the Crown, that the government should seriously consider paying its bills. The Temporary Wheat Reserves Act said that the Minister of Finance shall pay to the Canadian Wheat Board such and such moneys for grain in storage in excess of a certain amount.
The government ceased paying those moneys for 18 months. No legislation had been passed. The bill was before Parliament. It was a bill called Lower Inventories for Tomorrow, Operation Lift. Attached to the bill was the repeal of the Temporary Reserves Act.
When the court reconvened for the trial, the attorney for the Crown rose in his place and said that the government had withdrawn the legislation. I was here that night when the then minister rose and withdrew the legislation.
The Government of Canada and the Minister of Finance had to pay almost $100 million owing to the Canadian Wheat Board, which was money that belonged to the farmers of western Canada.
The courts have set a precedent in spite of the ruling of the Chair prior to that occasion. I would ask, Sir, that in arriving at a decision on this, the Railway Act provides for the payment of certain moneys under the at and east freight rate subsidy program. Those moneys have not been paid since last July. This situation, if not identical, is so close to it that it is not worth arguing about.
I would hope in light of what happened in the Federal Court that the Chair will recognize that and rule that the government can continue with its legislation which can take effect on the day set for proclamation or at the time of Royal Assent when it is signed by the Governor General, but it cannot be retroactive, and the government must pay the moneys owing under the at and east freight rate subsidies in Atlantic Canada back to last July. The government owes the money, it should pay its bills.
One correction, Mr. Speaker. My colleague from the Liberal party stated in his remarks that the Wheat Board had refused to pay over the money. That is not correct. The Wheat Board did not refuse to pay over the money. It did not have the money. The government refused to give the money to the Wheat Board so it could pay it out in a final payment to the grain producers. That is the history of that matter. I think it is a precedent.
The only exception would be a budget bill that sets a tax rate starting January 1 and passed in June. That is a precedent that has been long established in Parliament. Therefore, this situation is identical to the one in 1971 and has nothing to do with the budget.
Therefore, I submit that the Chair should rule that the government should pay its bills and that the bill is not in order although the government is acting as though it is already in force, retroactively to last July. Surely there must be something that we can do in this House, that the Chair can do, to make sure that the government obeys its own laws. If we cannot do that, we have anarchy. If we
February 13, 1990

have to go to court every damn time the government disobeys its own law, what is Parliament here for?
I put that question rhetorically and I urge you, Sir, to give this matter most serious consideration, which I know you will, and I hope rule that the government cannot act as though the bill has been in force since last July, and that it must proceed in the normal way before it can cease any payments under the at and east freight rates.

Mr. Speaker, on a further point of order. I would like to raise a concern I have with this particular motion. In reading the motion, it is not very difficult to make the assumption that it accuses this government of increasing regional tensions, increasing incidences of racism and increasing incidences of bigotry.
The point that I would like to raise is that if this particular motion referred to an hon. member the motion would be out of order because it would be making an accusation that would be considered unfair, unparliamentary and totally out of order. I feel the same way about this particular motion. I think that it is the kind of motion that is argumentative, abusive and casts aspersions on the government and therefore on members of this House. The motion should be seriously examined by the Chair because it is certainly bordering on poor taste, at the very least.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a brief word in opposition to the point of order being made by my friend across the floor. It is very clear that the intervention of the member shows a lack of understanding of what racism is about and how it works. Certainly the government is not being accused of being racist or of being bigoted. The problem is that the policies of the government are resulting in helping the cause of racism and bigotry. It does not have to be intentional and the resolution does not say it is.

February 13, 1990

I support this resolution and I am going to make the point when I rise of almost the inverse of what it is the hon. member has said. It is policies that may be well meaning, an attitude that might be defensible which is causing the unfortunate consequences that are contained in this resolution. I think that this is a resolution that contains an allegation that could be made against any member of the House, if the things that they were doing, although not in themselves racist things or acts of bigotry, lent support and comfort to others who were racists and bigots. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair and the Speaker have looked at this motion very carefully. What is coming out of the argument right now is debate. I think we should progress with debate. The hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, there are any number of approaches that could be used in a discussion of the issue contained in this motion. This motion and a previous motion recently debated in this House cover, as I will demonstrate, somewhat different ground. Perhaps at some future date we should have a resolution on the importance of ignorance in perpetuating racism and intolerance of the sort that was demonstrated by the hon. member on the other side. The motion states:
That this House condemn those policies of the government which, having bred a sense of insecurity, powerlessness and doubt among Canadians, are a cause of the recent increase in regional tensions and incidents of racism and bigotry in Canada.
There was a motion debated here on February 2. It was a motion moved by the hon. member for York Centre, a motion that our party certainly supported and one which elicited a good debate. That motion stated:
That this House condemns the intolerance and prejudice in Canadian society that damages the fabric of the nation and urges the government and all members of Parliament to play a role in strengthening understanding and respect among Canadians.
That debate was of the genre which had many members condemning the increase in frequency of racist incidents and examples of intolerance in this country.
If one briefly reviews some recent articles in Canadian newspapers, the cogency of that debate is well demonstrated. For example: "Teenager charged in the beating of a black". That occurred at Nova Scotia Community College. "Sikhs warn that intolerance should worry all Canadians. The sad resolution of Sault Ste. Marie. Minister blasts Calgary pins for promoting blatant prejudice. Organized group not suspected in white power posters. Sickening handbill declares open season on native people. Students reject turbans in the RCMP", and on and on it goes.
There can be no doubt that there was a reasonable basis for the concern that occasioned the motion moved by the hon. member. What we heard there were the heartfelt views of members of this House on all sides condemning racism, discrimination and prejudice. It is that kind of leadership which has provided Canada with a fabric of legislation, a Charter of Rights, and many other measures which express the best of all Canadian desires that there should be tolerance in this country, that there should not be discrimination, and that there should be, as much as we can provide it, equal opportunity for all Canadian citizens.
The acceptance of those principles, whether in law or whatever, is only part of it. Those principles have to be accepted by the people. By and large, they have been. There used to be the argument that there was no way in which one could change minds by legislation. Well, it may very well be that you cannot change the deep-seated attitudes of people. Many of us who have been involved in the civil rights movement in this country have expressed ourselves in terms of not giving a damn whether we change their heartfelt feelings that are not expressed. What we are concerned about is how people treat other people.
It may very well be appropriate to say that the motion we have before us is a reversal, in a sense, of the wording of the motion moved and debated previously in this House which stated that intolerance and prejudice damages the fabric of the nation. I think it is an appropriate paraphrasing of my motion to say that when the fabric of a nation is damaged, then one will have an increase in expressions of racism and intolerance.
February 13, 1990

There is a very important principle associated with the issue of racism and intolerance. It is a basic principle that if a nation is a civilized nation, if a nation is to be a tolerant nation, then the people of that nation must have a sense of economic security. They must have a sense of community. They must have a sense that they are determinants, to some degree, of the direction in which the nation will go. The moment that fabric is torn, people begin to act in ways which are offensive to those of us who believe in equality among all people, no matter what their differences. The principle we are addressing really is the principle of scapegoating. When people are hurt, when they feel vulnerable, when they think that they are going to lose their jobs, when they feel a sense of powerlessness, they begin to look around for somebody to step on, to blame and to act out their hurt.
There are many examples of this. Historically, in the American south there were those who were called "poor white trash". They were impoverished and they looked around to find somebody who was worse off, somebody to whom they could be superior. As anybody who has studied the situation in the south would know, that was an example of scapegoating.
Perhaps the greatest historical example of scapegoating was in Germany after the First World War. That country was undergoing tremendous social dislocation, unemployment and inflation were rampant. There was near anarchy. A leader appeared who produced the scapegoat and we know the dreadful results of that. If one reflects on what was said in Germany at the time, we must note what is happening in our own country.
There is a book described in The Globe and Mail as the cornerstone of APEC-I like to call it APE because it is so primitive-ideology. It is written by J. V. Andrew. This book is described as detailing Mr. Andrew's reasons for his opposition to French Canadians, described as a backward race that has taken over the province of Quebec to use as a breeding pen and marshalling yard for the colonization of the rest of Canada.
We say there are those who are absolutely committed racists, that they have little influence unless circumstances are produced that create that kind of doubt and vulnerability I was talking about before.
Supply
I noticed that just this morning someone of my acquaintance seems to have pre-empted the subject of my debate. It is an article by Robert White in The Globe and Mail this morning which states: "Current climate fosters intolerance." His description of the situation is as follows:
Increasing job losses combined with a shrinking social safety net leave people feeling less secure and more vulnerable to events over which they have no control. It becomes easier to attack the most vulnerable: women, children, people who differ from the mainstream by their race, colour, language or religion.
He also goes on to state, as described on February 2 in debate here, that the history of Canada has not provided us a solid record of tolerance and equality. However, increasingly over the years, in my lifetime, this country has become more and more civilized and more and more humane. What has distinguished us from our neighbours to the south is a sense of community responsibility, which is expressed in a variety of ways. It is expressed in the civilized way in which we have treated the question of basic language differences between the two colonizing peoples. It is expressed in an increasing concern about the status of aboriginal peoples in this country. It is expressed in the official policy of bilingualism. It also has been expressed in terms of such measures as unemployment insurance, medicare, and in so many other ways. This country has been based on the notion that there should be a mutual caring and that is fundamental in our society.
I submit to you that it is the erosion of that character of this country by the measures and policies implemented by this government which is largely responsible for what we are seeing in terms of scapegoating. One only need look at the examples in Ontario of those many municipalities that have passed resolutions declaring themselves unilingual. We know that this is in its expression racist, but what is the cause? The cause is that increasingly municipal councils are being asked to deal with problems with which they cannot fairly deal. It is part of the increasing unfairness in the distribution of responsibility for paying the cost of government. It is part of the unfairness in the tax system that the federal government fails to meet its obligations with respect to financing certain programs which evolved at the provincial level. In turn it goes down to the municipal level where the most regressive of all tax, the property tax, has to pay for it. People on the front line have to deal with these decisions for which no financial position was made.

February 13, 1990
Supply
What happens? A group of bigots give them the excuse to go around looking for a scapegoat. That is what is happening and that is what is going to happen to an increasing degree if we do not re-establish our commitment to the kind of society we want to pursue.
Increasingly, our country is a social democratic country. The reason I am a social democrat is that minority groups, linguistic groups, women, and all of those in our society who are so excluded are going to be the victims unless there is equality for all and unless there is a stake for all in the future of this country.
When we have the implementation of a free trade deal with which the majority disagree; when we have the niggardly attack on the unemployed with changes to UI; when we have a GST that perpetuates the notion that the rich should be relieved of the burden in favour of increasing the burden on the poor and the middle class; when we have increasing food lines all over the country; when we have people who are losing their jobs left and right; when we have regional disparity; when the fishermen know that their livelihood is at risk; and when farmers see their livelihood at risk, they look for scapegoats. People, having lost a notion of having any influence on the future, look around for others to blame. They are more immediate because they have a government that passes policies that are at odds with the views of the people and at odds with the view of what should be the destiny of Canada.
If one wants to look for the reason for increased racism, discrimination and violence then look for the increase in the sense of powerlessness that has been caused by a government that has ignored the people. It is committed to the powerful at the expense of the powerless.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened very closely to my colleague's statements and feel very close to this subject.
I would like him to look back on some of the more serious incidents of racial problems we have had in this country. There has been the internment of the Japanese, which I am close to since my wife was interned, the Chinese who had been singled out in Vancouver for such things as a head tax, and long periods where they were
refused immigration. Look at that in terms of the economic situation in the country and how people who were feeling economically disadvantaged looked to other people to find scapegoats for their own economic disadvantage.
Could the hon. member draw some insights into why people who are often poor and disadvantaged themselves look for easy scapegoats rather than looking to the system, the powerful and the people who are the real oppressors? Why do they always look to somebody else who is more defenceless than they themselves are? I think that is one of the dynamics that happens. Why do these people not insist that a government like this bring in equitable economic programs, programs that will guarantee employment, housing and all of these things, rather than simply make scapegoats of those who are less powerful than themselves?

I thank my colleague for that question. This is what I was saying in terms of the importance of a sense of powerlessness and vulnerability in producing scapegoats.
We all want to be able, in some measure or to some degree, to control our environment. We want to be able to work and have decent housing. When we see that that is not available or that is threatened, we have two choices. We can try to convince governments, agencies or institutions in the community, impersonal all of them, to respond to our need. If there is no response or perception that there ever can be a response, then one looks around for some means by which they can, however distorted the point of view, bring about change.
If there is a lack of housing or jobs and looking around one sees a black person, a Sikh or a francophone has a job, and he or she has not, well, since government will not respond, let us go and attack those people who have the jobs we think we should have. Never mind that they may be more qualified because there is another element in all of this. There is a message in being included in the group. It is very important for everyone to be included in the group. It becomes even more important to be included in the group when one is in the situation of feeling so vulnerable. Of course, it is nice to be in the majority. It is nice to claim identification with the more powerful because, always, a majority is more powerful
February 13, 1990

Marc Lepine looked around for a scapegoat under the same reasoning that women were depriving him of the opportunity for jobs in technology. We know the awful, brutal outcome of that perception of reality.
It is extremely important that governments at all levels have an awareness of the implications in what they do.
