In the case of Sault Ste. Marie there were decisions to be made with respect to costs that were passed down to the municipality. Collectively, the French-speaking minority of Sault Ste. Marie was attacked.
This entire package of actions by the government has in so many ways changed Canada and threatened ordinary people. These actions are a basis on which our commitment to equality in this country is called out of question because people look around for someone to blame and respond to as an easy target.

Mr. Speaker, Nelson Mandela is a free man at last. Although only for a modicum of 48 hours after 27 years of political imprisonment, the impact of his freedom on the people of South Africa and indeed on Canadians and the whole world has been profound. His freedom has evoked indescribable joy world-wide.
He has come to symbolize indomitable courage and unwavering moral conviction in the face of enormous political adversity and state imposed racial discrimination, also known as apartheid. He never ceases to inspire the hearts and minds of all freedom loving peoples to his ideals.
It was with the same ideals and courage that he first greeted his people and the world just after his release: "I greet you all in the name of peace, democracy and freedom for all". No doubt he will facilitate their attainment in his country for his people.
We in Canada must remain vigilant and supportive to ensure that Mr. Mandela's freedom and his struggle for his people shall not be a fleeting moment in history and that what we have seen in South Africa is the real beginning of the triumph of human dignity and the end to racial bigotry.

A new era of liberalization, unification and openness is unfolding.
As part of this historic process, Canada is now hosting the first international "open skies" conference, attended by foreign affairs ministers of 23 NATO and Warsaw Pact countries, the purpose being to negotiate a treaty autho-

rizing both blocks to conduct unarmed surveillance flights over each other's territory.
Other aspects of European security including the use of conventional weapons are being discussed. It was even suggested that the "open skies" concept be expanded to include surveillance of oceans and space.

Mr. Speaker, today the Innu nation announced that if the Government of Canada does not halt its low level destruction of their homeland in eastern Quebec in Canada, they will ask the Federal Court to stop the flights, as in the Rafferty dam case.
The government is destroying the Innu land and their hunting. It is claiming that no one lives there permanently. That is a lie. The Innu have lived there for 9,000 years, much more permanently than recent European visitors.
The government claims its environmental impact study proves no serious damage. That is a lie. Two groups of international experts have condemned the government's study as a worthless cover-up.
The government says it does this training to protect us and western Europe from Russian invasion. That is a lie. No one believes the Russians will or can invade us. Therefore, Poland, Germany and other European countries are reducing their low-level flight training. However, this government expects $2 billion worth of economic benefits to Canada from low-level flying.
I call on the people of Canada to demand that this government stop this shameful and greedy destruction of the Innu nation.

Mr. Speaker, tourism is an $800 million industry and growing in Nova Scotia. The industry wants support from government by way of marketing and other assistance. Most important, the industry wants a government that listens. This government listens.
Earlier this year the minister of tourism announced welcome federal support for Sea Sell '90, Nova Scotia's national award winning tourist promotion.
I wish to share with the House a letter I received this week from one of South Shore's major tourist operators referring to the minister's decision. He writes:
The decision is important for two reasons. It supports the efforts of
the private sector who are committed to the success of this project.
And, as important, the decision reflects that government is listening.

Mr. Speaker, the tourist industry is twice as important to P.E.I. than it is to any other province. It represents 10.5 per cent of our gross provincial product. Nova Scotia is second at 5 per cent.
In addition, tourism is the largest employer in P.E.I. The GST will, according to the Canadian Tourist Research Institute, harm P.E.I. more than any other province. For example, if an American comes to Canada, as an individual he or she can apply for a rebate of GST paid in Canada. This in itself will be a nuisance factor and a deterrent to the industry. But if the same person comes to Canada on a package bus tour, he or she must pay the GST to the tour operator who forwards it to the government. However, neither the tourist nor the tour operator can apply for a rebate.
Jim Larkin, executive director of the Tourism Industry Association in P.E.I. says the GST will hurt in many ways but will be especially damaging for American bus tours. The tax will make destinations to P.E.I. in Canada too
February 13, 1990

expensive for Americans. These groups will look elsewhere in the U.S.
In 1989, 1,062 buses brought 41,213 American tourists to P.E.I. They contributed almost $5.5 million to the Island economy. When reductions like this are added to the reduced rail service, reduced Tourist Canada promotions and a high Canadian dollar, one can see that a major Canadian industry will be in difficulty and another major source of income to the people of P.E.I. will be jeopardized.

The arrival of the Concorde proves that Pearson is an airport of international proportions. However, we cannot overlook the fact that the airport lies beside residential communities which are affected by airport activity. This must be considered every time a change is made at the airport.

Mr. Speaker, at the most recent meeting of Canadian ministers responsible for wildlife, held in Quebec City, the Minister of the Environment presented his provincial counterparts with a new action plan which the Environment Department is carrying out. This plan gives considerable importance to wildlife and its habitat, a subject in which all Canadians are particularly interested. The investigation which was done on this subject clearly shows that wildlife is a significant economic resource and it is interesting to note that 91 per cent of Canadians take part in wildlife-related activities, for which they spent over $5 billion in 1987.
Mr. Speaker, in Abitibi, we firmly support measures to conserve wildlife and its habitat.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw attention to this government's lack of effort in promoting Canadian seafood markets and export markets.
In 1983-1984, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans spent some $4.5 million on marketing. Since then, most of the responsibility for marketing has been transferred to the Department of External Affairs. The result has been that in 1989, $1.9 million was spent on seafood promotion under the program for export development. Not a very good record. Not only has the budget been reduced, the effort has been diffused within the much larger trade development program.
By its own account, the government has caused the current crisis by over-estimating traditional fish stocks. If the industry is going to successfully expand into the under-utilized species, the primary responsibility for market development must be returned to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Only as a result of a
focused and a well-financed program within the responsibility of that department most clearly related to fishery will this difficult transition be accomplished.

One internationally respected scientist describes it as the worst impact statement he has ever seen.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister show some courage and sincerity about the rights of the Innu and the environment of all Canadians and order an entirely new environmental impact statement?

Under this program 80,000 workers at Canadian airports were subjected to background checks and fingerprinting. A judgment released yesterday by Madam Justice Barbara Reed, ruled that this program was illegal and must be discontinued.
Oral Questions
Exactly what can the minister do and what does the minister plan to do for the protection of the Canadian travelling public?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was advised of Judge Reed's decision this morning. First, I would like to give Canadians the assurance that all this does not affect the security system in our airports which is operating normally. We intend to look at various possible responses to Judge Reed's decision.

speakerposition: subtopic
Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have received notice of a question of privilege from the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte.

Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege concerns smoking in the government lobby of this House. I must say, first, that I have never risen on a question of privilege before.
While privilege in the United Kingdom has always been based on common law, it has never been transferable to the colonies except by statute. The right of Parliament to establish its privileges is guaranteed by the Constitution Act, 1867. The most recent time that this was done was in 1985 when Parliament passed the Parliament of Canada Act in 1985.
I raise this question simply because I believe that in this House we are trying to set an example for Canadians, particularly young Canadians, and we are trying to establish a smoke-free environment for future generations of young Canadians. I believe we are falling down in that regard.
I point out that this House passed an amendment to the Non-Smokers Health Act in 1989. That act clearly requires that the House of Commons provide a nonsmoking atmosphere for its employees. Because we are the employers of a number of individuals in this House, including clerks, young pages and the personnel of all members of Parliament, I believe that we have a responsibility to ensure that the environment is maintained smoke-free.
The act defines "employer" this way:
"Employer" means a person who employs one or more persons in employment described in subsection 123(1) of the Canada Labour Code -
Under the definition of employer it states:
(c)	the Senate, House of Commons or Library of Parliament, in relation to employees thereof or employees of a committee of the Senate or House of Commons, as the case may be, or
(d)	a member of the Senate or House of Commons, in relation to employees on the staff of the member, including persons employed in the office of a Minister, or in relation to employees on the staff of a political party housed in accommodation provided by the Senate or House of Commons who are under the direction and control of the member;
In terms of our precincts-and I believe that I am absolutely correct in this regard-I wish to quote from Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, page 31, Citation 93(2):
Control of the accommodation and services in that part of the Parliament Buildings (the Centre and West Blocks, the Confederation Building and other buildings occupied on behalf of the House) and its precincts occupied by the House of Commons is vested in the Speaker on behalf of the House.
February 13, 1990

I also submit that the work and the performance of members of Parliament are being jeopardized because we are not adhering to that policy. Again I wish to quote from Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 16, which states:
The distinctive mark of a privilege is its ancillary character. The privileges of Parliament are rights which are "absolutely necessary for the due execution of its powers". They are enjoyed by individual Members, because the House cannot perform its functions without unimpeded use of the services of its Members; and by each House for the protection of its members and the vindication of its own authority and dignity.
To me, this is a very important matter. I know we are attempting to clean up the environment of this country. I do not think there is any better place to start than right in this House. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that you have set the example since I have been in this House by bringing to the forefront for Canadians the attention that the environment very clearly needs.
I am not doing this for vindictive purposes. I am a non-smoker. However, there are many members in this House who are attempting to give up smoking. It is very difficult for them under these circumstances. There are very many members of Parliament in this House who have respiratory problems, and they have real medical concerns. It is very difficult for them to function in the lobby which is an extension of the office of a member of Parliament.
In the government lobby there are a number of telephones and desks from one end to the other. When members are present on duty in this House, many of their hours are spent in that lobby working on behalf of their constituents. I contend that their ability to work and act on behalf of their constituents is impeded simply because of the environment in that the lobby does not allow some individuals to sit there and work on behalf of their constituents.
I take this matter very seriously. I believe that we too in this House have to set an example for all Canadians. Again I say "young" Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, you are very cognizant of this fact and have brought it to the attention of the House many times. When we members of Parliament get out of hand from time to time, you are always the first one to stand and remind Canadians from coast to coast, the people
Privilege
back home are watching us, that we are clearly under their scrutiny.
I believe that if we are going to honour the traditions of this House, then we have to do it by honouring a bill that was passed in this place by us. I believe that we have to do it in fairness to all members of Parliament. I believe that we owe it to ourselves to make sure, if we are attempting to bring in a bill all Canadians have to live by, that we as members of Parliament are willing to live by it ourselves.
Accordingly, should you find that a prima facie case of privilege does exist, I am prepared to move the appropriate motion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to share with the House some of the experiences in the other lobby, that is the opposition lobby.
Since the adoption of the law I must say categorically that I have received absolutely the co-operation of all members in our lobby. There has been no smoking in the opposition lobby since the end of December 1989.
I have not seen one member smoking. As a matter of fact, today I had the pleasure to hear the member for Halifax tell me that she has quit smoking because of the interdiction to smoke. I encourage her to continue in that respect.
If the member has a grievance-and I doubt very much that it is one that touches privilege-then I think he should bring it up in his own caucus as a serious matter of discussion for them to decide. What happens in that lobby is their business. If he has a grievance with them, I think he has to take it up with his own Whip or somebody else.

Mr. Speaker, maybe we could all help each other and contribute to solving this difficult situation by kindly asking the hon. member if he would, for a time, suspend his desire to have you rule on his question of privilege.
In the meantime, I would respectfully ask Your Honour to write again to all members of Parliament, as you do from time to time, to remind them of the new rules that are in place. I am of the opinion that many members are still of the opinion that they can smoke in certain places and not in others.

February 13, 1990
Privilege
I would suggest the hon. member suspend his request until Your Honour has had a chance to look into his question of privilege, as is his right. In the meantime the Chair can remind members of exactly what the law means and, if there is an exception, then you, Sir, will let us know. If after that time members do not abide by that reminder, then at that time I would imagine he would be more than anxious to rise again on the same question of privilege. At that time I am sure there will be many other members who would love to get up and participate in the debate that the hon. member may raise.
Of course I am in your hands, Mr. Speaker, with respect to whether or not you find my suggestion acceptable. I am also in the hands of my hon. colleague to know if the suggestion I just put to the Chair is acceptable to him.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same question of privilege. I sympathize with all those people on the other side who wish to smoke.
I would say that this is the first time I have ever seen any regulation come in when there has been no opportunity for people in a federal agency-and Parliament is a federal agency-who do smoke to receive any advice or counselling.
I am sure that soon the freight entrances will not even be available for some of the people to smoke in because it will be banned there too. There is absolutely no place on Parliament for a person to smoke.
I do not smoke any more, but I can certainly appreciate the plight of those who do.
I think this is a question of privilege that should be looked at from the point of view of there being nothing provided for people who do smoke.

Mr. Speaker, I know that this is an opposition day and that we do not want to prolong this matter for too long.
I was surprised that my friend raised this question of privilege because I know he is such a clean liver who has never been overexposed to lung problems, I guess, through smoking.
There is a problem here. We all know people should not smoke, but I quite agree with the hon. member for South West Nova. I did not hear all the remarks of the hon. member for Saint-Denis. However, I hope he was saying that the committee which he chairs ought to look into the matter. I think he is chairman of the members' services committee which quite frankly, and with all respect to my great friend, has been the most inactive cobweb committee around here for the last several months. It has not looked after the rights of members.
I quite agree. I think this is a classical situation. I used to be a practising lawyer, as I used to be a sometimes smoker. I never smoked cigarettes; I sometimes took a puff of a cigar.
Oh, oh!

Having been in both of those areas, Mr. Speaker, as you yourself once used to be a practising lawyer, you and I know that there is an old maxim which applies in this case. I will not say it in Latin because when I use Latin around here people think I am being racist. I like Nova Scotia as Nova Scotia. I do not like it as Nouvelle Ecosse or as New Scotland. But in Latin there is a good old maxim which when translated means that the law is an ass many times when it does not have basic common sense. You can say that in Latin but it sounds better in English.
I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, in all fairness-and I have written to you on this matter before-that I knew this regulation was coming in on January 1, 1990.1 do not think a lot of members around here did. Frankly I do not think we appreciated the stupid law that we passed which did not give rights to both smokers and non-smokers so that those who serve us have a place to smoke somewhere in this institution. There should be a place in all other federal buildings under our jurisdiction. The blanket, unilateral approach which has been taken makes all sorts of deceit possible.
In answer to the rhetorical question from the member for South West Nova, even now you get the ridiculous situation exposed to me and experienced by me on Friday of last week when I was smoking in the freight entrance with several other good colleagues and employees of the House. Some commissioner felt duty-bound to send his lower sabaltern in to tell the hon. member and all the other employees that, "Gentlemen, I hate to do this but you are not supposed to be smoking in there. Would you

please take a step and go out into the pouring rain and keep puffing out there?"
In answer to my friend, who is relatively new to this place, lobbies used to be the place in the whole institution where members on all sides and/or your own group would sometimes lobby, sit around, converse, socialize, meditate and think about some problems of state. Sometimes if they had the odd hiccup or had some social juice and/or sometimes puffed away, that sometimes helped in the meditation process so that some problems of state would be resolved.
I can tell you this, Mr. Speaker, and I am not trying to be too facetious or too humorous: the atmosphere around this place has changed, and not just because of no smoking. It has changed because of computers and fax machines and the personality of the whole political process now.
But when you add all those things together in the mechanical world and take away some of the companionship that some of us enjoyed in meeting with our fellow members in the lobbies, we do not do that any more. I want to raise as a question of privilege some day the fact that we should have a bell or a flashing light at the entrance way of all doors so that if we are puffing back there we can find out when the bell stops so we can get back here and vote.
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I really think this matter should be discussed by the members' services committee, not just by the members of Parliament and our staff, but perhaps hopefully by House leaders to show that if the regulation is in stone for all federal employees then something can be done so that there can be some smoking spot. The thing has gone too far. I understand the respiratory situation, health and all that.
But, goodness gracious, there is something else in Latin, caveat emptor, let the buyer beware. Let the smoker beware. With all the advertising through the federal government and everything else, we know smoking is not healthy.
When are we going to get away from big brother always telling us what to do and let individuals start to make up their minds? Let us give an area for those who do want smoking. For those who sometimes do want to partake in a bad habit, let them continue to partake in
Privilege
the bad habit on their own without big brother telling them what to do.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I just want to respond to some of the comments made here today. In particular as an aside at the beginning, if I may, I want to say that it is a wonderful picture the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants paints of this place in times past-no women, lots of men, everyone sitting around drinking and smoking the day away.
However, I would like to say that if my hon. colleague from Saint-Denis and his committee go forward with some recommendations on this matter, we cannot see these recommendations go forward merely for this sacrosanct institution of the Commons. The public servants of Canada who work and live in their environments around us, both here in Ottawa and across the country, would hardly be edified if there were special places for the employees of the House of Commons to smoke in comfort and not such special places for other public servants of Canada to smoke.
Having recently joined the ranks of the converted- and this is the second time I have done this on television, so I hope it works this time-I can say that these stringent laws have made it a little bit easier for those of us who want to quit. We also have to remember that in so far as smoking in the lobbies is concerned what we are doing is infringing on other people's air space, if you will.
I think a separate place where people could go of their own accord-and I think the legal term is volenti non fit injuria-is something that could and perhaps should be done. Certainly it should not just be for the House of Commons. It should be something that is done for the Public Service generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to spend a moment or two on this topic which has nothing to do with government legislation, as some of our viewers might feel it does, namely, Bill C-51.
I remind hon. members that the Speaker is obligated to follow the law. The law that was passed was Bill C-204, a private member's bill. Under a private member's bill, members of Parliament had to decide individually as to whether or not he or she would support that

February 13, 1990
Privilege
bill. There were no government Whips on that legislation. It was every member who decided for himself.
It was the former member for Broadview-Greenwood, Ms. Lynn McDonald, who brought in that legislation. I think viewers should be reminded and we should remind ourselves that it was not government legislation. It was the House of Commons deciding on a vote by each and every individual whether or not Bill C-204, which was a private member's bill, should be passed.
Additionally, what we should now keep in mind is that the Speaker by action of this Parliament is obligated to obey the law and to enforce the law here.
We know my good friend from Annapolis Valley- Hants well. We will not go into his personal views. He can say whatever he wants. He as a legislator as well is obligated to follow the law and expect the officers of this House to follow the law. It is for that reason I do not think the Speaker has any opportunity other than to follow the law set out in Bill C-204.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak very briefly on this matter. I agree with what the minister has just said.
I supported the law. I think the law has done a marvellous job in helping to discourage Canadians from smoking. However, as we pass laws in this place we have more of a responsibility than others who are affected by it to look at some of the impacts that the law is having.
For my part I prefer a smoke-free environment, and I am glad to have one provided for me. I have been trying in my own mind to come to grips with the problems of passionate smokers, committed smokers, people who seem unable-even knowing all they know about the dangers of smoking-to give it up.
I would commend to hon. members to think of committed smokers who are unable to give it up as people suffering from a form of handicap. Being addicted to tobacco is a form of physical handicap, whether or not it is significant that they are the authors of their own misfortune that they became handicapped through decisions that they made themselves.
I do not think their situation is really much different from other people who are handicapped and in a lot of cases may also be responsible for becoming handicapped.
They may have driven in a way that led them to becoming blind, paraplegic or something like that. We do not make a moral judgment about handicaps. At a certain point we have a responsibility and the Charter of Canadian Rights and Freedoms requires us to accommodate their problem.
As we begin to see some of the real suffering that people are feeling and the terrible inaccommodation that they are subject to, these people who cannot give up smoking, I commend hon. members to think of their plight and to try to find some other solution than to force them in a cold Canadian winter, as I saw this morning, to have to stand outside to be able to smoke.
I do not agree with smokers. I like sending a positive message and a bit of a kick in the pants to people who insist on smoking, giving them, as my colleague from Halifax noted, a real incentive to try and give it up.
But there is a limit. Now that we in this House are starting to see it among our colleagues and staff, I think we ought to try and think of a way of learning to live with what I hope is a dying handicap, one that 10 years from now will not be among us.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief comment. I hope we will all remember this moment as we pass other laws. It may be one of the few occasions on which all of us sitting in this House have occasion to live with the results of the laws we pass in a very real and personal way, whether it be as smokers or as people seeing our colleagues suffering through the problem of addicts deprived of their drug.
We imposed this requirement well over a year ago on every person who works for the Government of Canada. I doubt anybody in this House at that time considered the effect on those people, smokers or non-smokers, or on their productivity. This debate did not occur in this House until we ourselves were affected by it.
I hope we will remember this moment and with every law we pass think about how we would like to live with the impact of that law.

The law may be, as the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants said, an ass. Well we passed it.
I wasn't here.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McCurdy:
That this House condemn those policies of the government which, having bred a sense of insecurity, powerlessness and doubt among Canadians, are a cause of the recent increase in regional tensions and incidents of racism and bigotry in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot begin to express to you and the House my outrage on seeing the thrust of this motion which has the gall to accuse the government of pursuing policies that have contributed to the creation of racism and bigotry in the country. This is the government which had the courage to address an incident in our history which scarred our nation. I refer to the Japanese-Cana-

February 13, 1990
Government Orders
dian Redress Agreement. This is the government that established the Deschenes commission. This is the government that enacted the world's first multiculturalism act which recognized our rich cultural diversity as a fundamental characteristic of this society. This is the government which is establishing the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship to promote a vision of full equality for every single Canadian, and this is the government which recently introduced Bill C-63, an act to establish the Canadian Race Relations Foundation.
I am outraged, Mr. Speaker, and so are all those Canadians who are contributing to make this country a better place in which to live. While I do not like the motion, I am certainly pleased to be able to speak to it.
When I saw this motion, two things came to mind. One is the chance to inform Canadians of what this government has done to combat racism and bigotry in this country. The Prime Minister has made it clear that they have no place here. I could stand here for at least an hour or more and recite a list of the positive achievements in this area since 1984, but that would give this motion more credence than it deserves.
For me, this motion has no focus; it has no substance, and it has no sense. These are empty and meaningless words. The hon. Member for Windsor-St. Clair has put everything but the kitchen sink into the motion. There are statements here that must be addressed. Let me say that I welcome this chance to set the record straight today. I welcome this chance because the hon. member who put forth this motion is himself among the many hon. members who just last week sent back to my department a coupon asking for copies of all the materials about eliminating racial discrimination recently published by my department.
These materials are in the process of being distributed to our regional offices, institutions, government officials, leaders in the field of race relations, concerned citizens, individuals of all ages, backgrounds and origins throughout Canada. They know we care about this issue and they know we are doing something about it. Maybe the hon. member who proposed this motion could learn something from their example.
Since 1984, this government has worked to make this country a place where social justice, equality and national unity prevail. The Canadian Multiculturalism Act, which became law on July 21, 1988, responds directly to this essential challenge.

The Canadian Multiculturalism Act states that, in harmony with the recognition of Canada's two official languages, the multiculturalism policy must preserve and enhance Canadians' multicultural heritage and seek to achieve equality for all Canadians in the economic, social, cultural and political areas of Canadian life.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, the Act commits the Government of Canada to an active, energetic multiculturalism policy making our diversity and the challenges and opportunities it presents an integral part of the process of building our country.

The Canadian Multiculturalism Act takes us a step beyond the establishment of equality rights. It actively promotes equality. It strengthens our sense of the distinctiveness of the Canadian identity. It contributes to our better understanding and acceptance of each other. It commits the Government of Canada to ensuring that all Canadians can participate fully and without discrimination in defining and building Canada's future.
The policy and the ideals of the act unite Canadians because they have great hope and great aspirations for this country. Those are the people who have this great hope in it. They believe that we can have an even better and fairer country. So do I. Canadians are not afraid to meet the challenges of our society today. They do not agree with the negative and destructive picture presented by the hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair. They have a different vision of what Canada is and can be.
I am fully aware that we do not yet have a perfect society. In spite of progress there are still danger signals when we take stock of where Canadians are right now in their relationships with each other.
We are all aware of overt incidents of racial intolerance, prejudice and bigotry in our country. We have seen the headlines about the report on the Donald Marshall Inquiry, about a racist pin and the creeping incidence of
February 13, 1990

anti-Semitism, the blatant hatred of the Jim Keegstras and others whose names are less well known.
I am not new to the issues, the concerns, the facts and the statistics and I do have a sense of urgency about what needs to be done. I have felt the stinging barbs of intolerance and ignorance myself, but at the same time I have a sense of optimism and hope that Canadians are at their core decent and caring people who want nothing less than a society of true equality. That is why my department immediately worked to build upon the equality provisions and promises of the Multiculturalism Act, by making race relations and cross-cultural understanding a priority program.
In September 1988 I first announced a framework for national action in the field of race relations, a framework for change and for progress. This national plan defined six fronts for positive action. Many of you are familiar with them already. Let me share them with you again: public education, changing our institutions, helping voluntary organizations, generating more research about racism and racial discrimination and how to fight it, setting an example at the federal level, and getting governments to work together.
Changing public awareness is a major task. There are many activities in this area, but our most significant work in public education is centred around March 21, the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. I know many of you are familiar with this date and with its fundamental objective, namely to raise public awareness of equality issues and to get Canadians on side in the fight against racial discrimination.

For the first time in 1989, we had a large public awareness campaign for March 21, the International Day for the Elimination of Racism and Racial Discrimination. Many activities were held with the support of Multiculturalism and Citizenship Canada, as well as other governments, community groups, human rights groups and various other institutions.

Approximately 52 municipalities throughout the country participated in our first major March 21 campaign. I am very optimistic about the growing profile of this
Government Orders
effort. March 21, 1990, promises to generate even greater public attention and I see it as a most effective way of circulating our message in schools and communities throughout Canada.

We have clearly stated our purpose: Promote appreciation and acceptance of the principles of equality and multiculturalism among Canadians and in federal institutions and develop the will to implement them.
We recognize that, within our social structures, institutions have tremendous power. They can share in the life and work of every one of us.
To overcome racist attitudes, we must make structural and institutional changes.
The department which I head helps Canadian institutions adapt to the cultural diversity of our country. Thus, we encourage institutions to examine their structures and policies to detect obstacles to full equality of rights; these obstacles are not always obvious to those who run these institutions.

To that end, my department supports institutional change related to education, policing, the media, health and social services, labour and municipalities. Of course we recognize that in many of these areas, provincial and municipal governments are on the front lines. No real change can take place without their active involvement and so we are working closely with them.
I would like to mention a few of the key projects we have recently undertaken in partnership with others. We have been working directly with the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police to promote the development and use of cross-cultural training within police forces. Our efforts in this area, and in encouraging the recruitment of visible minorities, are essential if we are to make authority figures more representative of our multicultural reality.
This past summer a pilot project was established for visible minority youth in Vancouver who are interested in careers in policing. I met with some of these young men and women and I can say with confidence that this project was a great success.

February 13, 1990
Government Orders
In October I convened a national consultation on policing in a multicultural society. Federal and provincial officials from across Canada met with police chiefs and officials, along with representatives from visible minority communities. Together, we are finalizing a national action plan to strengthen police minority relations.
There is no room for racism in our places of work. Yet, all too often, the doors of our institutions are closed to some because of discriminatory attitudes. In addition to our ongoing efforts in the area, I am working to develop a national anti-racist education program with the Canadian Labour Congress. Together we are developing a three-year plan to provide training and education materials for the thousands of union shop stewards across the country.
It has been said that if Canada is a microcosm of the world, then municipalities are our neighbourhoods. It is certainly true that municipal governments are most in tune with their own local conditions.

That is why my department is working closely with municipal administrations across the country. We support the Federation of Canadian Municipalities through its race relations program. We have helped establish a national action committee on race relations. We have also helped to develop a series of practical guides on race relations.
I believe these publications have already had a positive impact.
We have made a major contribution to the second national seminar of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities on race relations at the municipal level, a seminar held in March 1989.
Another very productive federal-municipal initiative was the founding of the Hasting Institute in Vancouver. This agency will help the city adjust to the changes taking place as a result of the increasing impact of visible minorities, women, native people and the disabled.

Last year, Toronto City Council declared 1989 as the Year for Racial Harmony in an effort to sensitize the people of Toronto about issues of racial discrimination.
My department also provided support for this very worth-while municipal initiative.
We are working directly at the community level, but we are also involved with the gathering of better knowledge and information to help combat racism more effectively. Much has been done to achieve this objective, and much more will be done.
The government announced in the last Speech from the Throne that legislation would be tabled to create a Canadian Race Relations Foundation. That promise has been kept. The legislation is now tabled and we will be moving ahead as soon as possible to create a centre for research and action in this vital area; a centre which will work to help eliminate all forms of racial discrimination.
I have mentioned just some of our government's achievements. While it is clear that we have broken new ground and set new standards in certain areas, it is also clear that there is still much to do and we cannot do it alone. Government leadership is vital. But to achieve real progress, an entire society must be mobilized. A co-ordinated, co-operative approach must be put into place. We see today how the call for reform by people like Lech Walesa and Nelson Mandela has had a profound effect.
This kind of broadly based social action could not have been achieved without a groundswell of support at many levels. Real change is not achieved solely through individual gestures. It is realized through partnership. Here in Canada the federal government has assumed a leadership role in the area of race relations. But the actual effects of our efforts would be limited only to our government offices if we ignored the need for partnership.
"Racism" and "bigotry" are ugly words and their reality is uglier still. They are not things we as Canadians like to accuse one another of. We do not want to think of our society as discriminatory or intolerant. The fact of the matter is, however, that racism and bigotiy are part of the fabric of Canadian society and have been for a long time.
In the past, to our shame, we have too easily and too often side-stepped or simply ignored these issues. To our credit, I believe that those days are over. At the same time, however, I believe all of us involved in the elimination of racial discrimination must be very clear about what it is we are trying to achieve. We are not trying to achieve a tolerant society. Tolerance is putting
February 13, 1990

up with something, accepting it, living with it because there is no alternative. We have to move beyond tolerance.
Racism is not going to disappear overnight just because we recognize and comprehend that it is offensive to the dignity of all human beings, but we must expose prejudice for what it is, the act of bigotry, pure and simple, and once so isolated, we can and will eliminate it with every resource available to us.
As I have said in this House on previous occasions, the issues of combating racism, prejudice and bigotry are ones in which I have a deep personal involvement. In my youth, I felt the weight of that oppression and I resolved to fight it. I have done so in my community, in my neighbourhood, and now, here in Parliament. That fight is not over. It will not be over until we have eliminated racism, bigotry, and all forms of racial discrimination in Canada. We must do this task together. We must do it now, because together we are better.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the minister. I do not want to take anything away from his commitment to fight racism. I also do not want to take anything away from the list of measures he has put forward as achievements on behalf of his government. However, I wonder if he agrees with me, as does the member from Windsor, with the sense that we have that for everything the government says it is doing, things seem to be getting worse on the racism front and one does not have to look very far for examples.
There is a question I want to ask him. I will have an opportunity to speak, and I would like to be pointed about it, because I really think input on this subject could be valuable. More than action, there is a responsibility on people of good will and on governments to react to things when they happen. Something important happened in April 1988 as an example to which the government has failed to react to this day. A reaction by the government would have measurably supported harmony across our country, certainly in the part of Canada where it arose.
I am referring to the efforts that have been made by the Sikh community to get their religious artefacts and obligations recognized and accepted as part of the fabric of Canadian society. I am talking about Canadians here who have a right under the Charter to practise their
Government Orders
religion, a right which is protected by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
They appealed to the RCMP to allow them to wear their turbans on the job and in their dress uniforms. If the answer were no, they would not be able to serve in the RCMP.
Religious obligations have to be tested in the institution against the practical requirements of that institution. The RCMP made that check and they could not come up with a practical reason why Sikh religious observers should not be allowed to wear their turbans. They looked at it and could not find a reason. They could not say safety considerations, environmental considerations. There is no reason why those individuals who profess the Sikh faith should not be entitled to wear a turban in all aspects of the performance of their duties in the RCMP. Commissioner Simmons came forward in April 1988 and said that there was no practical reason why a turban should not be allowed as part of the daily uniform, as part of the dress uniform.
The government has not responded. They have not said, as the Solicitor General is supposed to do: "We will go along with your interpretation of the law. We will make this contribution to understanding and harmony within Canadian society." They have been silent for 1988, silent for 1989, and silent until today, except that a few days ago I heard the Solicitor General saying that he was looking for a compromise. I would like to know what he meant by that.
However, more important, I would like the minister for all of the goodwill and all of the good things that have been done to recognize a substantial failure by this government, by members of the government, by the Don Mazankowskis of the world, to stand up in western Canada where they are respected, and in other parts of the countiy where they are respected as well, and stick up for a decision such as that which would have done a great deal to promote better harmony and better understanding among Canadians.

I have a sense that this type of episode, much as other types of episodes that have been occurring far too frequently across the country which my hon. friend is indicating are bothersome to him as well, are part of an over-all crisis. The crisis is one of national identity.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
There is some difficulty in Canadians understanding what our fundamental characteristic is. There is the linguistic duality of the country, of course; our protection of minority rights and how that harmonizes with our multicultural reality. I have certainly spoken to how that diversity strengthens and unites us.
There is a lot of work that we have to do in helping Canadians understand what we have become. I said that I cannot do it alone. I said that the government is committed, physically and personally, with this very strong cross-government commitment to examine how every one of its departments and institutions can better reflect our diversity. I have been building partnerships with other levels of government. Indeed, I have been reaching out for partnerships in the labour community, in the business and non-voluntary sector, in the health and social services, among others. It is quite obvious that all of our institutions do not reflect to any great degree the rich diversity of our nation, so a lot of work has to be done.
There are a lot of people of goodwill and understanding out there. It is an issue where we have to be generous and bring a lot of understanding. Last Friday I brought forward a committee of very distinguished Canadians who represent the different walks of life to help advise on how the Multiculturalism Act could be better implemented, to provide public accountability in a very open manner to Parliament and to advise me on what we are doing. All those representatives will help within the sectors they come from so that their own sectors can better reflect our diversity and allow us, once and for all, to have full equality and full participation, which is the minimum we can expect for our citizenship.
With regard to any specific incident that takes place, I have developed initiatives to address those concerns in a very proactive manner. The situation that the member has raised is one that I have certainly discussed on
numerous occasions with my colleague. I have even heard the minister respond that-maybe he said it in self-reflection-perhaps the delay has not been helpful to what he had hoped would be necessary in his resolving the issue. I did what I had to do to be helpful and now we are looking forward with anticipation to the minister making his decision, which he said he would do some time this month.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am really quite shocked at the distortion that was contained in the argument of the minister with respect to the motion before this House.
I was quite clear, but of course the minister wrote his speech before he listened to the debate, that there was no criticism contained in the motion about those specific measures and the will of the leadership of this country in respect to legislation and any number of acts that are intended to attack discrimination directly.
If the minister does not understand what was contained in the argument this morning then he ought to be ashamed of himself. The classic source on prejudice in Canada, The Vertical Mosaic, pointed out the importance of scapegoating to the question of racism and discrimination.
I should also point out to the minister that this motion has to do with something else besides racism and bigotry. It has to do with regional division. The minister may not agree with me, but he has no excuse to distort my argument. The argument is quite simple. It is the position of the New Democratic Party and of a great many thinking people in this country, and he came close earlier when he made reference to the sense of lack of control that is growing in this country, that this government, by its policies, has attacked the very fabric of a countiy that has had a sense of community out of which has come that legislation that bans discrimination, that is intended to discourage prejudice.
No amount of legislation in the world will prevent the acting out of racism, if the people acting out their racism have not got a sense that the country belongs to them, that the country cares for them, and that the government cares for the country. If there is a feeling out there that that sense of community is being lost, that there is more generosity to those who are already rich at the expense of the poor, if there is a sense that the regions are
February 13, 1990

suffering at the expense of the more prosperous regions, if there is a sense that government is acting on behalf of some at the expense of others, if those who are vulnerable are threatened with lack of housing, lack of employment, by God, my God, Mr. Minister, you bloody well ought to know by now, if you know anything about the issue, that scapegoating will result. That's the argument that we should debate.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us today focuses on the same issue in a way that I raised on behalf of my party in a resolution on February 2. It calls on the House to condemn those policies of the government which have bred a sense of insecurity, powerlessness and doubt among Canadians, are a cause of the recent increase in regional tensions and incidents of racism and bigotry in Canada.
In the resolution I put forward a little over a week ago, I laid a responsibility on all Canadians and on Parliament to take stronger measures to combat racism. This resolution focuses particularly on the responsibility of the government and that is exactly what I would like to do in the course of the opportunity I have to make some remarks today.
We are fortunate, in looking at the problem of racism, in that Canada is not a racist society. We have racism here, but we also have a great well of decency across Canada and we have the willingness which we have expressed time after time after time as a nation to combat racism when we see it. We have passed laws. We have established commissions. We have set up the Court Challenges Program, which I hope will continue to be funded, although the government has not indicated that it will. We have people in the field, we have resources from the private sector, all devoted to trying to eliminate racism from Canadian society.
The main way in which racism can be eliminated in Canadian society, and the sense of it that I want to bring
Government Orders
to government responsibility, is the responsibility to exercise moral suasion as individuals, as decent people in the society, and for the government, on its behalf, to try to fight racism and counter it when we see it.
My contention is that for all the lists of achievements of the government, for all the programs and so on, they are not providing the kind of moral leadership that would make a difference in Canada today if they would provide it. It can sometimes be expressed in terms of race or nationality. Sexism, it seems to me, is often an expression of that same phenomena of hatred, fear, anger and contempt.
In the sense in which I have just defined it, what has been happening more and more in Canada is a small group of racists, whether it relates to language, sex, race, or whatever, has seemed to develop an evil genius, a kind of a genie du mal, de la destruction which leads them to develop the capacity to animate a large group of Canadians who do not have that characteristic and who are not racist in the sense that I just defined but who are disgruntled. There is a lot of disgruntlement in Canada now. There is a great disappointment in this government and I do not say this to members opposite in a partisan sense. It is a simple fact drawn from statistics and reactions to the programs and policies of the government. There are disgruntled people out there. There has been disgruntlement expressed with provincial policies in some parts of the country. All of that together provides a pool that the evil genius of racism has been able to animate and mobilize to lead to attitudes that are very destructive to the essential fabric of Canada.
Our country is more vulnerable to that type of attack than other countries because we are not the monolithic expression of one culture or one language. We are a mosaic, a patchwork, a quilt, to use Jesse Jackson's expression from the United States, of a lot of different groups. Cement to keep those groups together is a vital necessity in our national life. As groups that are motivated by racisms of one kind and another attack the fabric, we need to respond and react.
As I said a moment ago, when I was talking to the minister, it is not only actions. The minister piled up a large list of impressive things that the government has done to combat racism. The main thing that needs to be

February 13, 1990
Government Orders
done is to stay in touch and in tune with that fabric and movements that are going backward and forward which are threatening it in one way or another and to respond to them. It is urgent in this fabric of Canada that there be that kind of response whenever it is needed. Leadership needs to be provided.
I will digress for a moment to make the point that the government does know what leadership is. The government has shown leadership. It has shown it in the economic area. No one can say that it does not have an agenda, that it is not serving certain interests, that it does not have certain goals. I do not agree with it. My party does not agree with it. I do not think most Canadians agree with it. But the government knows what it is doing over there. It knows who it is working for and what it is trying to achieve. The government does not do it just by bringing in legislation. There are speeches, the government has programs, and it is back and forth across the country talking up economic policies which it has. But when it comes to the area of moral or social leadership, that is where the leadership that we see them capable of giving in some other areas is not given. To that extent, although I am showing some differences with my colleague from the New Democratic Party about the way I see the problem, the leadership that could be provided to help keep the fabric of Canada strong is simply not being provided.
I want to make my point by talking about the language issue. The language issue is a tough, tough issue for Canada. What is often not mentioned in debate is that our country was founded because we were able to make an agreement that accommodated French and it would not have been founded without it. We made a commitment to the survival of French in Canadian society. It is right there in the British North American Act of 1867.
Some people say, "Well, we made a deal in 1867. We will stick to that deal, but don't ask for more". That is not good enough. I think most Canadians know that, because unless there is more and we have richer programs and responses to the French fact in Canada, it will not survive. The commitment that we made in 1867 was to the survival of French and in one way and another the official languages policy-

-is a reflection of our commitment to accommodate and ensure the survival of the French fact in Canada, not just in Quebec but in Canada. And I think that is what should be the basis of our response.

I sometimes listen to the phone-in shows on the radio. You hear people saying "Well, there are more Italians in our town". Or "There are more Germans in our town than French. What are we talking about the survival of French for?" I would like to hear people reply more forthrightly that Canada exists because of the commitment we have made to French.
This is not to say that Italian is not an important and interesting language. I speak it, I enjoy it. It is a very big part of the cultural life of my city. But it is not in the same category of national commitment as our commitment to two official languages. I wish that was realized more across the country when people look at the methods that have been devised with great consensus in this House to support bilingualism across our country.
A few Ontario municipalities, too many of them, have gone unilingual, to coin a phrase. This is very disturbing because it sends a bad signal. It shows you the kind of evil genius that is behind it, although I am certainly not critical of everyone who supported it. I think a lot of them were in the category of groups animated by a cause that gave them an opportunity to express their dis-gruntlement. At the heart of it is something veiy evil.
This APEC, the Association for the Preservation of English in Canada is meant to give a kick in the head to the concept that the survival of French is a valid concern. The people who thought that up are saying, "You want French to survive. Well, we want English to survive and here is our association to do it". There is a very big difference between these two causes. One makes absolutely no sense. There is no basis on which one can argue that the survival of English is in doubt in Sault Ste. Marie, Thunder Bay or in any municipality in Canada or anywhere in Canada. English is a language which is surviving and thriving.
When you look at the issue of French survival I think it is a different story. A small island of six million on a continent which is vastly anglophone, little communities across the rest of Canada outside Quebec where in their daily life French speakers cannot operate in French only.
February 13, 1990

This is a real problem. When APEC comes along with that wonderful name, Association for the Preservation of English in Canada, it is the most terrible insult to concerned francophones who legitimately want to see their language preserved. We are talking about something valid compared to this idea that the survival of English is somehow threatened by any of the bilingual policies that one has in place in Canada or that you could think of. To me, it shows the nature of the source of that movement across Ontario.
I think we should fight it. You hear some saying that they are doing it because of what is happening in the province of Quebec and they are coming to the aid of the poor anglophones in Quebec who have had their rights limited by Bill 178.
[Translation \
I have already condemned Bill 178. The use of the notwithstanding clause was something to be deplored. I think we had to make this eminently clear, and we did so. Perhaps we should look at what Quebec Anglophones have to say.

I have a letter which was sent out. It is addressed to the citizens of Sault Ste. Marie and sent by Alliance Quebec. Do you think that Alliance Quebec is saying "Thank goodness you are finally giving those francophones in Ontario terrible treatment". That is not what they are saying in this letter. They are saying the opposite. The Alliance Quebec people, who speak English themselves, want the Association for the Preservation of English in Canada to stop.
I would like to table this letter. First, I would like to read a part of it:
I urge you, as citizens, to put pressure on your elected officials to reverse their decision. In doing so, you would be honouring the past of your community, which as its name implies, is built on the site of an old French trading post. Sault Ste. Marie is a reminder of the pioneering spirit of our French and English forebearers who built this country together.
At a time where relations between English- and French-speaking Canadians are strained, you have an opportunity to make a gesture
Government Orders
towards greater harmony. I hope you do not let this opportunity pass.
Ask your City Council to reconsider this matter now.
That is how the anglophones in Quebec, who have suffered to the extent that they have-

-with Bill 178. This is in reaction to those who seem to help by denying, at least symbolically, the rights of francophones outside Quebec.

This is a wonderful kind of Canadian gesture by Alliance Quebec. It is signed by Robert J. Keaton, President. I would like to commend them for doing that.
I want also to deplore the developments of last week in the House of Commons on this very subject. My former leader, the Right Hon. John Turner, on his last day as the Leader of the Opposition, brought forward a simple, straightforward resolution which I have here and which I would like to read.
I would have thought in the light of Sault Ste. Marie, and in the light of Alliance Quebec, with the Thunder Bay vote coming on and with the need, as I mentioned, for cement for national unity within the Canadian mosaic to be provided in a reactive way when it is needed, and not just when it is time for the Speech from the Throne.
The leader brought forward this motion:
That this House reaffirm its commitment to support, protect and
promote linguistic duality in Canada.
Now there was a resolution that should have whistled through at two o'clock. I spoke to the mayor of Thunder Bay, Jack Masters. He told me, and maybe we need to be told this in the House of Commons, that it would have made a difference across our country if the House of Commons had passed a resolution on that subject. People care what we think in this place. They are affected by the kinds of ideas, exchanges, the things we come to terms with here and the resolution that we make of them as members of Parliament.
That simple resolution did not get through because the Prime Minister of Canada chose to play politics with it a few days before the by-election in Chambly. I would be happy to discuss this further. I see members opposite thinking I am being unfair. I am not. Instead of adding to the resolution in a way which would have reinforced it, the Prime Minister of Canada added some baggage to it,

February 13, 1990
Routine Proceedings
acceptable to many members of Parliament, including myself, but as he well knew, not acceptable to many others.
I talked earlier about another example where the government should have come forward. I had a chance just a moment ago to ask the minister about it. I am referring to the Sikh turban in the RCMP issue. I do not want to repeat what I said a few moments ago, but I cannot help but reflect on the quality of the hand-ringing answer that I just got from the Secretary of State on why it is that when the Commissioner of the RCMP made the statement, which was really a legal declaration in April of 1988, that there was no basis in law for denying the religious expression to the Sikh community.
There were many ways it could have been looked at. Many arguments could have been made. Do you need a turban for safety reasons, or the helmet, or whatever? He went through all that because our Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not give a person the right to express every right when it is not reasonable in a free and democratic society.
So the commissioner was looking at what are the reasons that we can say; "You cannot wear your turban". He could not come up with a reason. So he said; "Okay, you can wear them". But then it fell to the Solicitor General to give a simple order and I have had the honour of having that office. If he had given the order at that time, "I approve of the use of turbans by religious Sikhs in the RCMP", I think the atmosphere in western Canada would have been very different. I do not think the button campaign would have been launched if people like the minister from Winnipeg, the minister from Calgary, ministers from Edmonton, members from every community, had stood up and said that there is no way we can or should stop the Sikhs from wearing their turbans in the RCMP. If that type of animation, leadership, and moral suasion had been exercised, Canada would be stronger today. That is why I agree with this resolution and that is why I join in condemning the government for its policies.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend brought up the issue of Sikhs in the RCMP wearing turbans. I would like to pose a question to him because a lot of people in Alberta are struggling with this very concept.
One hears a number of arguments. Some of the arguments are that it is heritage, custom and so on. I do not agree with that personally. Another which is also put forward is that the reason police officers wear uniforms is to distinguish them and in no way should uniforms show or point out a religious position of the individual wearing the uniform. There would be situations where an officer of the law could be arresting an individual of a different faith and there could be real animosity on religious grounds between the individuals. If a change in dress of any officer points to the fact that he follows a certain faith, whether it be Sikh or Muslim or whatever, this could cause problems for the officer and also problems for the individual.
If the police officers in Ireland were identified by religious differences that could cause a lot more turmoil than really exists. I would ask my hon. friend, through the Speaker, if he would consider this a valid argument.
Supply

Mr. Speaker, I do not consider it a valid argument, although I know a lot of people feel that way. To me there is enough uniformity left with the rest of the dress when the headgear is changed. A person with the uniform would be clearly identified as a Mountie. The Mounties have very high standards. They do not pick just anybody to join their force. I believe that the public would know when approached by a turbaned Sikh wearing a Mountie uniform that they were dealing with an individual who met the high standards of the RCMP and not someone who was inclined to be prejudiced in any way.
I make a counter-argument to the member. That argument could be used for arguing that blacks or Indians should not be allowed to be in the RCMP. Although their distinctiveness is not expressed by clothing, it is expressed by characteristics and colour of their skin. All of the arguments you made about what kind of prejudice might be assumed could be tied to the colour of their skin as well. So, let us not have it one way and let us not have it the other way. The Mounties have high standards. They are not going to hire people who do not share their high standards. I think the public will accept a member of the RCMP with black skin, with Indian racial characteristics, or with a turban on, and they will accept him up to the high standards of the force.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard the hon. member speak in many areas of the country on the issue of human rights. He is, without a doubt, one of the leading exponents of this issue. Given that, I wonder if he would comment on the Marshall report within the context of his earlier remarks.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member. I know he has shown in all of his public career a great concern for issues relating to native justice and aboriginal rights. He raised the question of this report with me when it came out. I want to tell him I feel I could have used that as an example just as strongly as the other matters I mentioned.
When the Marshall report came out, I got up in this place to ask him for action, the Minister of Justice said: "We are waiting for the Province of Nova Scotia to take action". I would have liked to have heard a different answer from the Minister of Justice. In the context of social activism and leadership, the right response would have been: "This is a devastating report and here is what

the federal government is going to do on its side of it". The Marshall recommendations were there and there were a number of them that the federal government could have implemented.
We have had the reaction of the Government of Nova Scotia for one week, and one could say a week later: "You said you were waiting for the Province of Nova Scotia to respond. Now can we hear from you?" Another week has gone by and we have not heard.
Leadership and reaction are extremely important ingredients to fighting this war on racism which every society has to fight but even more in a multicultural society. I rate the government very lowly on reacting to these issues and I think observant Canadians do also.
