I would just ask my hon. friend about his response to the hypothetical situation I posed to him. He indicated that it could be colour, or along the same line. I would answer that by saying that colour does not determine a man's religion. Religion, as you know, can become very emotional.
There is a case in Edmonton of the city fathers wanting to put a cross at intersections, a painted cross on the pavement where someone had been killed in a traffic accident. Because this had religious significance, other religious groups became very emotional about this and said: "No, we will not allow this. It is not right, because it is a religious symbol." The city of Edmonton had to change and not put a cross, but now paint a coffin. I am putting it in that context.
These are the arguments that many of my constituents and many of the people of western Canada are making.
It is not just changing the headgear. The headgear in itself becomes a religious symbol. That is where the problem arises, not because of heritage. I personally do not care if they change the headgear. But the headgear itself is a religious symbol in the same way as a cross would be a religious symbol. This is the problem that people are discussing and one that I think we should address.

Mr. Speaker, I think the city is wise to use another symbol than the cross to signify where people have been injured in traffic accidents. I know this was the policy in Belgium and in Europe. What they had was just an outline of a person on the sidewalk. This, to me, is an area where there is no religious requirement, that you use a cross to make that symbol on the road. You can do anything. But with observant Sikhs they cannot, consistent with their religious principles, go out without the turban on.
The question is, are we going to accommodate their clear and demonstrated religious observance or not? We have a law on the subject. The law says that we recognize it unless, in a free and democratic society, there is some reasonable basis on which we should not. And there is not, so far as wearing the Sikh turban is concerned.
I was on some hotline shows in Alberta and I know the kind of concerns people have who are not racist. I hope the member noted in my remarks that most of the people who are behind these causes are motivated by others. I feel that at the centre of it, there are people who are animating others because of fear, hatred or contempt which leads them to animate others to take positions on some issues that are veiy divisive of a multiracial, multicultural society like Canada.
I ask the member, when thinking about the issue, to distinguish what is essential to religious observance and what is not, because the essentials are protected by our laws.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in this debate today. I will be sharing my time with my hon. colleague from Burlington.
February 13, 1990

I am pleased we are discussing this issue today because it gives me an opportunity to set forth the actions our government is taking to promote freedom, opportunity and tolerance in Canada.
The motion put forward today by the New Democratic Party does nothing to enhance that cause. In fact, it is a motion designed to promote discord and dissension. I find it disturbing because I believe, and this government believes, that it is up to all members of Parliament and all Canadians to do whatever we can to bring Canadians together. Indeed, it was the former member of Parliament and Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John Diefen-baker, who introduced the Canadian Bill of Rights nearly 30 years ago.
The Bill of Rights begins with five simple yet powerful words: "I am a free Canadian". It is those words that must and do guide the actions of this government. Our programs and our policies reflect the fact that all Canadians share the same rights, the same freedoms and the same opportunities. That is what makes this country so different from so many other countries around the world.
We have all watched incredible changes in the world over the past year. But the underlying feature in nearly every event in eastern Europe and in many other countries is the triumph of freedom. People from around the world are experiencing for the first time freedoms that Canadians have enjoyed for over 120 years.
When our government came into office in 1984, we committed ourselves to putting an end to the bitterness and pain all too many of our fellow citizens endure. We have dedicated ourselves to finding new ways to stop the process of polarization among our own people and to end the senseless divisions that are perpetuated every day based on the arbitrary notions of superiority and inferiority, replacing them with the healing wisdom of compassion and understanding.
Since this government has assumed office we have come to appreciate the dimensions of the problem, and I can say with great confidence that the personal effort on the part of the Prime Minister and all of his cabinet colleagues is testimony to our efforts to end the vicious cycle of racism.
Supply
We have provided not only a leadership of ideas, we have backed them up with concrete programs and federal initiatives. I can also say with pride that our government has done more to fight racism than any other in our history. All hon. members should be joining with us, working with us, in that great struggle. Racism is inexcusable. It is the policy of our government to work constructively with all Canadians to eliminate these evils.
Our record is one to be proud of. The Minister has pointed with justifiable pride to initiative after initiative of the anti-racism front. I would be glad to file with the House of Commons the press releases of those initiatives that have taken place in the last few months.
I underline the importance of those initiatives. Of course, we all have to be resourceful and tireless. In the Secretary of State and Minister of State for Multicultur-alism, we have a tireless champion for equality and fairness for all Canadians. His personal record is clear and his commitment to combat racism and prejudice is solid.
The fight against racism is part of our government's policy of multiculturalism. In 1988, Parliament unanimously passed the world's first Multiculturalism Act. This act clearly states that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society and that cultural diversity will be considered in all aspects of the decision making of government. It points the way to a Canada of equality, a Canada where understanding and acceptance is the basis of our relations as a people, in which the government is committed to ensuring that all Canadians can participate fully and without discrimination in defining and building our country's future.
Multiculturalism, for our government, is a policy that has solid programs and services. It is pro-active, antiracist and is in keeping with the objectives of the act.
But our government has moved beyond simply enacting the legislation. We have been actively working to ensure that the principles of multiculturalism are applied to the policies, programs and practices of all federal institutions. The elimination of intolerance and discrimination is today one of the highest priorities of Canada's multiculturalism policy and, indeed, will remain so.
The government and the members of Parliament cannot do it alone. It can, however, help bring together individuals, organizations and institutions to create a

February 13, 1990
Supply
positive partnership to build understanding and equality. Through those partnerships we can meet the participation and service needs of ethnocultural and visible minority community Canadians in special need of assistance. When they have to deal with institutions and practices they do not know or understand or when they have to communicate in a new language, we will be there.
At heart multiculturalism is about recognition that this society is for all the people who live here, all Canadians. That participation and opportunity must be equal in this pluralistic society.
The Multiculturalism Act itself is a central element in our striving for equality. Its fundamental aim is building co-operation and developing support for the equality objectives which are set out in our Constitution and human rights laws.
Multiculturalism seeks to preserve, enhance and share rich cultural diversity. We have established chairs of ethnic studies, and encourage various artistic and literary expressions as well as programs of fostering cross-cultural understanding. We are working to integrate Canadians of all background into the common life of our country, its institutions, its cultural vitality, its media, its political groups and its movements. This government has had the courage to tackle the sensitive, complex issues of Canadian identity and partnership and tried to lead all Canadians of goodwill to a better understanding of each other and their aspirations.
Our Multiculturalism Act is a symbol of that commitment to bringing Canadians together on a basis of justice and fairness. Canadians recognize that our diversity of traditions and insights brought together in our neighbourhoods, our schools, our businesses and in our civic forums is the rock solid basis of our strength. I am pleased that the Scarborough Chamber of Commerce has recently set up a multiculturalism committee in this respect.
Of course we still have much to do, and safeguarding equality for all will be with us for a long time into the future, and that of the generations to come, but we are indeed making progress and it is this government that has led in facing up to the problems and pointing the way to overcome them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond today to the rather serious accusations by the hon. member from the New Democratic Party. I regret that I have only a short time to argue against his vague criticisms.
I would like to refute the hon. member's motion with particular reference to the immigration program by arguing that the government is innocent of the charges we face today. Our immigration program engenders fairness from its very foundations.
When we talk about bringing people to our country and helping them settle, this government is guilty only of promoting equality of opportunity, justice and racial harmony. Entrenched in Canada's immigration law is the complete ban of discrimination on the basis of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sex. Section 3 of the Immigration Act requires immigration rules and regulations for admission to reflect standards consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
From the beginning, those people who wished to come to Canada are granted the same treatment throughout and fairness is guaranteed from the moment that anyone puts his or her foot in the door of the immigration program. At the same time, this government realizes that many of the new immigrants are personally disadvantaged when they first arrive in our country. They may not speak the language or understand their rights. New skills and understanding must be conveyed so that they have the same opportunities as all Canadians. They need assistance in adjusting to this new and foreign society so they can begin to contribute what they have to offer.
Most important in fitting in to a new community is the ability to communicate. That is why Employment and Immigration is spending $77 million this year for language training for new immigrants destined for the labour market. Furthermore, the minister has committed $2.5 million for language training for women who do not intend to enter the labour force. It is precisely these language skills which will pave the way for successful integration by these immigrants.
February 13, 1990

Besides language training, Employment and Immigration Canada assists some 130 volunteer organizations to counsel and support immigrants in adjusting to Canadian society. This can include anything from learning how to fill out a job application to understanding our laws and our government.
This year some 13,000 immigrants will benefit from the $56 million in funds for these programs. We should note that such programs often teach Canadians as much as they teach new immigrants. By working with people of different cultures, Canadians gain increased understanding and tolerance. Our host program is one such example where Canadians give of their time and understanding to help refugees settle.
Accepting people from vastly different backgrounds is indeed something to which Canadians have become accustomed. In recent years we have seen more and more people coming from countries in eastern Asia and Africa. Furthermore, in this year's immigration plan the minister has allowed for the resettlement of 26,000 refugees in line with our international obligations.
Canadians will continue to welcome the world's disadvantaged. While their backgrounds are foreign to those of many Canadians, their presence provides us with an appreciation of our life as well as an insight into the plight of the refugees abroad. Indeed, as the composition of our society changes Canadians have had to adjust their picture of what Canada looks like. As they tune into reality they discover that, as always, immigrants offer much to the quality of life and the culture of this country.
Everyone in Canada has the right to equal treatment and the opportunity to contribute. Through our programs and laws immigrants to Canada are assured those same rights that we have. By the same token, Canadians themselves are guaranteed equality of opportunity through our immigration policies. They are guaranteed equality of opportunity to work and opportunity to receive proper health care, education and countless other benefits.
One need only think of the scientists and the physicians and business people whose choice of Canada as a home has provided so much in view of the background from which they came. In view of the fact that we want
Supply
immigration to continue to meet the needs of Canadians, the minister is now engaged in an extensive cross-country consultation on immigration levels. Through discussion with sectors such as business, labour, health and social services and education, the minister will be assisted in setting the country's immigration levels for the years 1991 through 1995.
The House should note that these consultations serve a great educational purpose in themselves. Many Canadians who have never discussed the issue are now actively engaged in the dialogue. It is our hope that a more understanding public will emerge through these consultations.
Canada has earned a global reputation as a country that treats its new citizens fairly and justly. That reputation was recognized when the people of Canada were awarded the prestigious Nansen Medal. Our immigration program has a unique give and take nature. While immigrants are granted equal rights and opportunities, Canadians benefit from their presence in countless ways. It is the openness and generosity of the program and people that have allowed a vast mixture of cultures and races to exist peacefully in one country. We are the envy of the world in that regard. Levelling ambiguous charges towards the government's efforts as the hon. member has done today is entirely unproductive. The hon. member himself has done a great deal to foster racial understanding and better equality of opportunity.
Canada's immigration policies have been scrupulously careful about the need to promote racial harmony, equity and justice for everyone. I would ask the hon. member to recognize that fact.

speechtext: Before I recognize the hon. member for Vancouver East, I would just like to indicate that because it is the NDP's opposition day the rotation of the order is NDP, P.C., Liberal. There were two 10 minute speeches by the P.C., then the NDP, then the Liberals and it goes back to P.C. so that we can get as many speakers in as possible.

Mr. Speaker, by law Canada is a multicultural society with a charter that guarantees fundamental rights and freedoms. The present government which was supported by all parties in the House reaffirmed multiculturalism policy in a Multicultural Act a couple of years ago. This act, of

February 13, 1990
Supply
course, promotes multiculturalism and equality for all Canadians particularly in regard to federal institutions.
In light of this unanimous support within the House for multiculturalism it is rather sad to read a recent article by Maclean's magazine which shows that the popularity of this policy is declining. We hope this will be temporary. I would like to quote a couple of paragraphs:
- Prime Minister Mulroney - reaffirmed Ottawa's commitment to the multicultural mosaic-in a 1987 pamphlet that Canadians should have the freedom 'to retain their respective identities while joining one another as equal partners in a united country.' But the Canadian reality has clearly fallen short of the ideal. In fact, recent opinion polls show that, far from living up to the principle of ethnic harmony, a growing number of Canadians express intolerance not only of identifiable minorities, but toward the idea of ethnic diversity itself. The mosaic is under siege.
They mention also that polls show that when Canadians are asked specifically whether they support official multiculturalism most, about 63 per cent, still answer in the affirmative. However a Maclean's Decima poll shows that fully 61 per cent of Canadian respondents, including a majority of every income and education level, says that immigrants should change their culture in order to blend with the larger society.
Clearly this means that we must have a fairly aggressive program to develop equal opportunities in the real meaning of multiculturalism that will be accepted by and for all Canadians.
Not only is enthusiasm for ethnic diversity waning, but racism continues to be a disease of our society, as many people have pointed out today. Studies show that racism indeed is on the increase. In 1988, 70 per cent of people who were surveyed said they thought immigrants bring discrimination on themselves.
Although we have legal protections under the Charter and employment equity laws, systemic discrimination continues even in our own public service. It is appalling to think back to the past year when we witnessed the controversial killing of two blacks in Toronto, the racist theories of Philip Rushton, the 15-year cover-up of the murder of Helen Betty Osborne in Manitoba. We know that injustices against Donald Marshall cannot be wiped away with an apology.
In Vancouver feelings were inflamed against immigrants from Hong Kong, and skinheads have reappeared. Two years ago backlash was strong against boat people who sought refuge in eastern Canada, and I must say that some of the government policies did not alleviate that.
Here in the House of Commons we have had many petitions presented opposing the wearing of turbans by Sikhs in the RCMP. Our party believes that the Solicitor General has exacerbated this problem by delaying a decision which in very simple terms should be in favour of a policy which must conform to the religious freedoms which are guaranteed under our Charter of Rights. There should be no debate about that.
Racist pins in Alberta have promoted opposition to visible minorities, immigration and multiculturalism. Now we find this is spreading to anti-turban T-shirts and calendars which are being sold. Why can the Minister of Multiculturalism and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who lives in the city of Calgary, not have some influence and give some leadership to discourage this kind of trend? I think it is incredible that even the Chair of the justice committee has taken a stand against our Charter of Rights on this matter.
. (1650)
A more subtle form of systemic discrimination is evident within the government itself. The Canadian Human Rights commissioner a while ago strongly criticized the low proportion of visible minority workers that are employed in our own federal Public Service. Only 1.58 per cent of civil servants are visible minority people, compared to 6.3 per cent in the general workforce.
The government targets have not been reached at all. Government policies which established low targets and budget cuts certainly will curtail new hiring opportunities. We can predict that this kind of systemic discrimination within the Public Service against people of colour will continue.
It is absolutely essential that the government take leadership to establish a fair target for employment and promotion, not only of visible minorities but of natives, disabled persons and women. The Treasury Board should be setting the example within our own Public Service.
February 13, 1990

I want to give two examples of public servants who have had experiences of racial discrimination. They are Canadians whom we as members of Parliament have hired. I am ashamed to have to give these examples. Mary Pitawanakwak, an Ojibway Indian woman, worked for the Secretary of State. A human rights investigator confirmed that a public official had called her a "God damn Indian''. She was fired in 1986, two years after filing complaints of racial discrimination and sexual harassment on the job. This matter is still being contested.
A second example is the Canadian Alliance for Visible Minorities claim that Mr. Idris Ben-Tahir, a career public servant since 1963, has been a victim of racial discrimination. Although he is highly qualified, he was relegated to a position requiring Grade XII education, and was dismissed from his job as a senior technical editor with the Canadian Forces. After being exonerated by the military and Pubic Service investigators, he returned to employment and has continued to face harassment, and has become ill as a result.
The Canadian Alliance for Visible Minorities has recommended several points that they asked us to raise very strongly in the House of Commons. I do this on their behalf today. They have recommended that Ben-Tahir be appointed to a position in the Public Military Service of Canada befitting his qualifications and experience. Second, they recommend that Ben-Tahir be financially compensated for mental anguish, humiliation and harassment. Third, they recommend that an impartial inquiry be initiated to investigate the discriminatory practices directed against public servants from visible minorities, such that it may result in the development of an integrated strategy that would effectively identify and eliminate racial and cultural discrimination within the Public Service.
I repeat that this is our own Public Service and our own government which is condoning this kind of discrimination. The Alliance also states that this case is in direct contravention of statements made by the Prime Minister in a speech called "Racism is a Moral Enemy of Justice", in which he professes stringent actions are needed against racism in Canada. He stated:
If we fail to accept our individual responsibilities as citizens of
Canada, we fail democracy itself.
Supply
I could not agree more.
I ask the Prime Minister and the government, why he does not insist that action be taken to remove systemic discrimination in the Public Service of Canada.
What is the cause of these increasing tensions and the increasing incidents of racism and bigotry which are symptomatic of a sick society, as well as of sick people? We believe it is government policies to a large degree, as stated in this motion, that contribute either directly or indirectly. The cumulation of regressive, harsh policies has placed an increasing burden on individuals and families in various groups and regions in our society.
This is the kind of atmosphere that sets the stage for hostility, intolerance and for scapegoating of powerless people, as my colleague has said. We have layers of regressive and stressful policies which this government has imposed. We have yet to suffer the goods and services tax and an even tougher new budget. We are developing a society that favours the powerful and exploits the powerless. This is the natural breeding ground for racism and scapegoating and intolerance.
Free trade threatens our sovereignty, our Canadian way of life and our jobs. Interest rates are rising. Our dollar is fluctuating and business and consumers are suffering. Lack of affordable housing and high rents are a problem in many areas, certainly in my region of Canada, and people tend to blame and resent newcomers as a result rather than resenting the lack policies that should be solving that problem. Cuts to unemployment insurance and the erosion of social programs, family allowance, pensions and our health care system are government policies that are creating insecurity about the future.
Families need child care, and single parents and children are suffering from poverty. Many people in Canada feel that their children will not have a future as the costs of education rise and employment prospects are diminished. As a result, they often resent newcomers.
Privatization, deregulation and anti-union policies also are negative forces. Regional tensions are growing. The west feels isolated and left out. Eastern Canadians are struggling for survival. Northerners have been denied a say in our Constitution. Quebec wants acceptance as a distinct society. Growing reaction to the Meech Lake

February 13, 1990
Supply
Accord and minority language rights is largely a result of an insensitive government approach.
Yes, Canadians feel a lack of confidence in this government, a lack of stability and a worry about the future. This can be translated into anger and resentment that is projected in many directions. When people's security and livelihoods are threatened, when they face increasing debts and financial burdens, when they worry about their kids, and cannot find a decent job or affordable housing, the frustration and bitterness can turn to rejection and intolerance of those round them. I see it in my riding of Vancouver East every day.
Increasing waves of immigrants from Third World countries become an easy scapegoat, particularly in our large cities. Instead of blaming the government for high interest rates and inadequate housing programs, people often scapegoat the new immigrants, some of whom seem to be able to afford expensive homes.Inadequate public education is another very real cause of misunderstanding and prejudice.
I particularly want to praise Black History Month, which I think is something we should be sponsoring with all ethnic communities so that we have the true history, in a positive sense, of the contribution from various ethnic communities in Canada. It should be part of school curriculum.
The Multiculturalism Act requires participation of visible minorities in all federal institutions yet, unfortunately, Bill C-18 has not even mentioned this as a function of our new Multiculturalism Department.
I want to mention visible minorities on TV. There has been a positive increase in this policy, as commentators and talk show hosts and actors project a positive image which somehow infiltrates into the psyche of viewers. I think this is a very positive trend that should continue, and the CBC has a special responsibility.
Let me summarize several government policies that have a particular impact on ethnocultural communities and which are not helping the whole problem of respect for ethnic minorities.
Disadvantaged people need a voice and an advocate to speak for them in Ottawa. This is why advocacy groups like the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, NAC, NAPO and other groups are so important. Yet, last year the
government cut funding to advocacy groups by 15 per cent, and over three years this will be up to 50 per cent.
Again, this is really taking a voice away from powerless and disadvantaged people. These deep cuts seem to be especially targeted to limit the power of groups who speak out for change and represent the views of those disadvantaged people. It is an attack on the powerless in society who are struggling to achieve greater equality and therefore it is a blow to democracy.
Termination of the Court Challenges Program is another very serious problem. The government must continue this program so that the Charter cases involving discrimination against ethnic minorities and disadvantaged people can be heard.
Settlement and adaptation of new Canadian programs are essential for promoting racial harmony, as well as for helping immigrants themselves. Language classes and pre-employment programs should be expanded, not cut. I want to mention particularly the cancellation of the Citizen Instruction and Training Program in April which will make it very difficult for immigrants to get language training. In B.C., 83.3 cent of immigrants have used this program.
Without these programs new immigrants are prone to isolation, ghettoization and racism because they will not have the language skills and understanding of Canadian values to help them participate fully. Backlash from Canadian born citizens is more likely to occur the more that newcomers remain isolated.
This is an example of another policy where the Government of Canada bears a direct responsibility if this trend continues, and I urge it to finance programs adequately. It is an investment that is well worth it in terms of our future.
I could mention many other programs, and I did last night in the late show. There are concerns that our immigration policy is not fair, that it establishes two classes of immigrants: those who can pay to invest money and buy their way into Canada and therefore require fewer points, and those who have to wait for a long time and often cannot get into Canada.
Economic insecurity is one of the major causes of racism and intolerance in Canada. Government policies which will impose a 7 per cent goods and services tax on all Canadians and which will introduce a tough new budget will add to the anxiety and hostility of Canadians. We can predict that regional tensions will increase and
February 13, 1990

racism and bigotry, unfortunately, may continue to grow. Of course race relation programs are important and needed, but the government also must look at the basic cause and its role in creating an economy and a society that contributes to it.
We call on the government to consider very seriously the lack of confidence that Canadians have in this government in all regions and the negative trends that are growing in Canadian society. We urge the government to ease the burden on Canadians and to bring in a budget that is adapted to the needs of ordinary Canadians and disadvantaged people.
We particularly demand that citizenship and settlement programs, programs that promote multiculturalism and advocacy and those that eliminate racism and inequality, be adequately funded.

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to make a brief comment to which the member may want to respond.
I listened carefully this afternoon to the first speech from the member for Windsor-Lake St. Clair and also to the member for Vancouver East. There are some things being said that I take great offence to being a member of the government, and I want to mention a few of them because I think it is very important that they be brought forward.
First, it would have been much more beneficial had the original motion been phrased in a much more positive tone. I think the very fact that the motion is worded the way it is turns it into a very partisan matter, and the issue is far too important to be dealt with in a partisan manner.
The member for Vancouver East, as well as the member for Windsor-Lake St. Clair in his speech, talked about the free trade agreement threatening our sovereignty. That is a subject of debate. I do not feel that way.
Members opposite perhaps feel that way. I do not. I do not think it threatens our sovereignty, and I think it is outrageous to say that the free trade agreement somehow breeds racism and bigotry. It is absolutely outrageous. I certainly do not feel that way. I will not take a back seat to any member of this House in supporting
Supply
minority rights and visible minorities. I just will not accept the suggestion that since I strongly support the free trade agreement I am somehow a racist and a bigot.
The Charter of Rights and Freedoms was mentioned by both of the NDP speakers as well. One thing I did not hear them mention was that the Constitution currently has an override clause. Neither one of them mentioned the notwithstanding clause which threatens the rights of Canadians to freedom of expression, freedom of association, freedom of assembly, freedom of religion, freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, freedom from arbitrary arrest, and freedom of equality. Those rights are all threatened by the notwithstanding clause in our current Constitution. In my opinion that is a much greater cause of concern.
To conclude, the member mentions the funding cuts to different advocacy groups. Of course, for every dollar that the government has to spend there is probably $20 or $30 in demands from different groups that want funding. There are difficult decisions that have to be made. It is easy as an opposition member to say: "Yes, we will fund every single organization that wants money from the government", but there simply is not money there.
To criticize the goods and services tax in the next breath does not make sense. We cannot have a tax on one hand to raise funds and on the other hand say that we cannot cut spending anywhere else. There is only so much money out there for the public to pay.
In conclusion, I agree totally that ignorance does breed racism and bigotry in Canada. It is there. It has perhaps gone underground because Canadians will not tolerate open bigotry and racism any more, hopefully.
Ignorance also applies to government programs. There is great ignorance out there about government programs and policies. A recent poll commissioned by The Globe and Mail and CBC concerning the Meech Lake Accord is a perfect example. Some 71 per cent of Canadians do not know what the Meech Lake Accord is or what it stands for.
It is very difficult for me, as a Meech Lake Accord supporter, to defend the accord when ignorance exists. I think it is incumbent upon myself and all members of this House to explain programs like that.

February 13, 1990
Supply
Many of the things the member for Vancouver East and her colleague, the member for Windsor-St. Clair, say are subjects of debate. I feel quite differently about these things. I do not think the free trade agreement, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Meech Lake Accord and the goods and services tax breed racism and bigotry. I would be interested in her comments. I feel one way; she feels another. I am not a racist and a bigot because I support these government programs.

Mr. Speaker, I know the member is very sincere because I have worked with him on committees. I would like to thank him particularly for mentioning the notwithstanding clause. That was an omission in my remarks, and I think a very important one. It is one that minority groups, certainly in British Columbia, are concerned about and have formed a coalition to rescind Section 33.
The member is absolutely right. The danger is that any province or government using this clause could in effect veto the rights under Section 15 of our Charter. I agree with the hon. member completely, and I am very glad he mentioned that point.
As to the other points, what the government members have not heard or maybe do not want to hear is that we are saying there is a whole combination of repressive measures which have put a great stress on this country and are making people feel very unsure of themselves as Canadians.
Free trade is one of them. It is not that it specifically promotes racism. I do not think I said that. It is a combination of things that is changing our country. The free trade deal is promoting in my view the kind of dog-eat-dog society where competition and profits are the main motivation. We are in danger of becoming Americanized and losing many of the things that are a part of our Canadian value system. That is really why I mentioned that.
The member mentioned the Charter of Rights. Of course I did not say that the Charter of Rights contributed to racism. I think the Charter of Rights, on which I worked very hard with a lot of groups, is a very important step forward in Canadian society. Flowever it does not mean anything as long as civil servants face discrimination as our own employees and as long as we have people
experiencing racism in other ways. It is nice to have it on paper, but that is all it is for the people who are involved in those incidents.
With regard to cuts to advocacy groups, I would like to point out that the groups I mentioned are long-established coalitions that have the support of affiliate groups right across the country. They are vital in my view and in the view of most Canadians that know about them in presenting the views of the powerless people. They have been very useful, I know, in some of our committees in helping us to understand the impact of proposed legislation. It is very important that they be sustained. It may be even more important than building new bureaucracies like the Department of Multiculturalism.
We do not have money for eveiything. Let us put it into community services so people can speak for themselves, rather than bureaucrats in increasing numbers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I see that my colleague has a lot of interest in minority groups, but I was very disappointed when she started to mention the GST and such things.
I must bring to the attention of my colleague that I was an immigrant in 1953. If she compares where we were in 1953 and where we are after the progress of the last five years, she will see that we are in paradise here in Canada.
The hon. member talks about the GST. All immigrants from around the world know about the GST because this was not invented in Canada. It exists in all these foreign countries. I feel sorry that she has to mix partisanship in this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say that there are always exceptions as my colleague mentioned earlier, because somebody got such and such a thing. She must know that exceptions happen every day. We, in the Italian community, have just been involved in a specific case. It does not mean that the laws are bad. In the yellow pages published by Teledirect, Platon College in Montreal had substituted the word "mafia" for "Italian" in a list of 22 languages taught. If this is not discrimination, what is it? But one such case does not mean that the laws are bad.
February 13, 1990

So, even with free trade and the GST, I can testily today in this House that it is a privilege to be a Canadian or an immigrant in Canada. I would like to mention it to my colleague because I am one of them.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to live in Canada. I think we have one of the best countries in the world and we are very privileged to live here.
However, that does not mean that there are not negative things going on and that we as Canadians do not have an obligation as the Prime Minister said-and I quoted him-to do something about this, every one of us.
As far as the GST is concerned it is not only my partisan position. Millions and millions of Canadians across the country, everybody we talk to, are concerned about GST and the impact it will have on them. As I pointed out, this is one of many programs that puts great stress on people, particularly lower income people, and that really does promote negative feelings in society.

Mr. Speaker, today we debate the NDP motion:
That this House condemn those policies of the government which,
having bred a sense of insecurity, powerlessness and doubt among
Canadians, are a cause of the recent increase in regional tensions
and incidents of racism and bigotry in Canada.
I can certainly personally testify that I have seen a tremendous increase in regional tensions and incidents of racism and bigotry in this great country, Canada, of which I am so proud to be a citizen.
I do sense increased insecurity, powerlessness and doubt among many Canadians, but I question whether it is necessarily the policies of the government that have contributed to this, but rather the attitude and the lack of commitment to principles underlying many policies, not just this present government but previous governments have brought into being, which are at the source of the tensions, racism and bigotry in this country today.
In my own riding I have seen doubt rising over the English-French issue in our country. Anglophones are being talked to about a French threat and the division, the dissension, the bigotry and the tension have risen alarmingly and are of great concern to me because I see
Supply
them not only in my own riding but reflected across this country. I consider that our country is in considerable danger and its very existence is threatened because this particular tension has arisen.
Because of the international debt that we have in this country we have seen many changes to programs, the drawing back of programs that have brought security and freedom to people. As those programs are withdrawn and new taxation programs are imposed upon the people making life more difficult and more painful for Canadians, I believe we that we are seeing a lashing out by the Canadian people against this pain. It is expressed very often in xenophobia, a fear which increases tension and ultimately leads to racism and bigotry.
The bigotry, however, does not refer only to issues of racism. I am thinking, particularly, of the problem of poverty in this country. I recognize a lot of bigotry that surrounds the issue of poverty. As has been reiterated so many times we have one million children in this country living below the poverty line. We have many single parents with children. We have many working families with children who are living at or below the poverty line for whom life is very, very difficult and becomes increasingly more so every day.
As we have heard before in this House, now in the great city of Toronto, Canada, central Canada, the rich part of Canada, we have more food banks than we have McDonald's outlets. This is a disgrace for this nation. I was involved in establishing and working with a food bank program in my own riding some years ago. It was alarming to me to see the bigotry which was expressed in my community against those who were poor.
Much of that bigotry was expressed by some although not by any means by all of the volunteers who were there to serve the poor. The poor were criticized for smoking. They were criticized if they had a glass of beer. They were criticized if they took their children to a fantasy farm for some enjoyment where it cost a few dollars to enter. There was a lot of bigotry expressed against the poor.
I feel that because of a lack of commitment to principles in this country, principles of equality, freedom, understanding and tolerance, these people are experiencing increasing bigotry because of poverty.

February 13, 1990
Supply
The government has failed in speaking out on principle on many of the issues of tension within our country. I felt that the response by the government to the French-English problem was much too late. I personally addressed letters begging and imploring our Prime Minister, our Secretary of State and other members of Parliament to say something, to speak out about the benefit we have in our country through our bilingual policy. It contributes immensely to our country that we have a bilingual and a multicultural policy. We cannot let those policies sit on paper only. We must constantly safeguard those policies, speak out to defend them.
I am very concerned about what has happened to our Court Challenges Program. I sit on the Standing Committee on Human Rights that reviewed the Court Challenges Program. I was one of the authors of the report of that committee which recommended that the Court Challenges Program be continued, not curtailed as has happened so suddenly and unexpectedly during the last few weeks. Our recommendations were that this program be given sufficient funding to carry it through to the end of March 31, 1990, this year, when its mandate terminates. In addition, we recommended that more funding should be found for the program to carry it through to the year 2000.
The Court Challenges Program allows groups and individuals in this country to address minority language and equality rights issues before the courts of this country. It is a program that is essential at this point in time as our new Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which came to this country in 1982, is addressed and implemented.
It is most alarming that the Secretary of State, when questioned about this program, said that he could not convince his government, members of cabinet or his caucus to agree to the recommendations of the standing committee. It sounds as if we are to wait for a budget. The budget for the Court Challenges Program is certainly not enormous, but the benefit of the Court Challenges Program addresses every individual in this country. It is a basic right in itself at this point in time in assuring that people in fact know what their rights and privileges are as citizens of this great country.
I was very alarmed today to read this article in The Ottawa Citizen which to me again testifies to a lack of commitment to principle. It represents an attitude of the government which I think is at fault. I believe this is the source of the problem, perhaps more than the policies of the present government. This article is entitled "Advocacy groups fear they're being muzzled". The article says:
Public servants at the National Council of Welfare were recently silenced with strong hints their $310,000 budget was in jeopardy, according to sources, after they made negative comments about government policy-staff at the National Council of Welfare were told by-deputy minister for Health and Welfare, that the council's budget could be in jeopardy if they continue to criticize publicly in a time of restraint.
This, Mr. Speaker, in a country where freedom is a basic liberty for all of us, a basic right. It continues:
Council staff director Ken Battle has frequently criticized the "clawback" of family allowances and old age pensions as the beginning of the end of universality of social programs.
Andrew Cardozo, executive director of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, believes his outspoken criticism of the government's employment equity programs may have deemed his group "unreliable" in ministerial circles.
The council, which represents 38 ethnic organizations across the country, receives $200,000 a year from the federal government. Cardozo is braced for a cut this time around and fears the government will only finance projects it approves.
"This means the government decides what issue you can speak out on and which issues you can't."
I say that this again is indicative of a non-commitment to the principles of freedom, equality and justice in this country, the freedoms that underline our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I would like to challenge the government to change its attitude and to take advantage at all times of opportunities to speak out and defend our basic rights and freedoms to make this a country that all Canadians can take pride in and maintain in good order for future Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak to the motion that was introduced by the member for Windsor-St. Clair. It reads:
That this House condemn those policies of the government which, having bred a sense of insecurity, powerlessness and doubt among Canadians, are a cause of the recent increase in regional tensions and incidents of racism and bigotry in Canada.
February 13, 1990

Racism affects everyone, not just the new immigrants and the visible minorities. Although they are affected most directly, racism affects everyone. It leads to hatred, discrimination and tensions which in turn leads to violence whether physical or mental.
Racism is a force which destroys the very fabric of any society. It divides communities and prevents friendships. It is inimical to a democratic society like ours, yet it does exist in Canada today. It exists in our schools and in the workplace. It exists in small towns and cities.
Fortunately we can still say that equality of opportunity, social justice and tolerance and understanding are accepted as hallmarks of our Canadian multicultural society, but unfortunately injustices and intolerance still exist in the form of racism.
I recall the Betty Osborne murder in Manitoba which went unsolved for over a decade and the Donald Marshall wrongful conviction which again went undetermined for more than a decade.
Acknowledgement that racism exists in our country will enable us to work together to solve the problem. When racism is eliminated Canada will be a better place for everyone.
I would like to cite some recent examples of racism in our country. I cite the case of Mr. Idris Ben-Tahir, a visible minority who started his career as a public servant in 1963. Since his wrongful dismissal in 1978 he has been subjected to harassment. Although both military and public service investigations where he had worked have found that he was dismissed without cause, today the Department of External Affairs has not yet made any concrete efforts to move him to a position that is in keeping with his academic background and practical experience. What a waste of talents we allow to happen. Despite his impeccable credentials, Mr. Ben-Tahir is relegated to a position requiring a much lower level of education.
Turning to my second example, I am appalled at the racist reaction toward the Sikh community that has occurred as a result of the positive efforts of the RCMP to allow Canadians of Sikh origin who are members of the RCMP to wear their turbans. Canadians of Sikh origin should not have to abandon the religious tenets
Supply
that are the cornerstone of their way of life to serve the people of Canada in the role of an RCMP officer.
The RCMP and other police forces have recently recognized the need to be more responsive to the communities they are charged with policing, including our ethnocultural communities. That is why efforts are being made to recruit officers from the different groups, and for this I would like to laud the government. This is a progressive step. Without it, charges of racism and discrimination against the RCMP like those levelled against some provincial police forces could occur.
The government, by its inaction on the RCMP recommendation to allow Canadians of Sikh origin to wear their turbans in the force is in effect refusing to allow Canadians of Sikh descent to wear their turbans in the RCMP and therefore we are discriminating against their religion. We are not allowing unlikes to be unlike and yet to be equal before the law. We are forcing unlikes in terms of religion to conform to likes or else to suffer negative consequences.
Turbans and ceremonial daggers are obligatory tokens of the Sikh faith. Any baptized Sikh would not be able to join the RCMP if he is not allowed to wear the turban. The existing dress code is an infringement of their rights under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The government must accept the recommendation of the RCMP, and soon.
I now come to the issue of discrimination against our aboriginal people. The 1988 annual report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission stated that the situation of the aboriginal people in Canada is in many ways a national tragedy. I quote from that report:
The grand promise of equality of opportunity that forms the
central purpose of the Canadian Human Rights Act stands in stark
contrast to the conditions in which many native people live.
This assessment is at once obvious when we examine our justice system and the representation of natives in the workforce. Native Canadians are over-represented in our prisons, but under-represented in the workforce. This situation is ugly at best.
A 1988 Canadian Bar Association report shows that slightly over 10 per cent of the inmate population in federal penitentiaries comes from the native community. Yet natives make up only about 2 per cent of the

February 13, 1990
Supply
population. It is therefore apparent that the general legal system is heavily weighted against the native population. The bias in the system must stop.
The almost uniformly non-native face of our police forces must be changed. Even if this is changed, there will still be non-native officers dealing with native citizens. Hence the entire police force must understand the context of native culture and the concerns of native Canadians. It is necessary to help ongoing cross-cultural training programs at the policing level. They are also necessary in the court system and in correctional institutions.
Natives do not just face discrimination with the justice system, they are also discriminated against in the field of employment. Employment equity reports confirm that native peoples are drastically under-represented in employment in almost every industrial sector and occupation. This is the case even in places such as Winnipeg where there are large native populations. Sadly, even within the federal government where programs to promote native hiring have been in effect for some time, the representation of native peoples is unacceptably low.
There are other areas of federal responsibility in which the government could do more, not less, such as has been stated. Our Court Challenges Program should ensure the pursuit of minority rights and equality for all. Language classes should ensure the participation of new immigrants and citizens in social and economic spheres. Citizenship classes should be made available so that immigrants can apply for full citizenship so that they feel fully part of our country.
The government could do more in the area of ethnocultural groups which could advocate the rights of new citizens and immigrants, as well as in the area of settlement programs, loans to small businesses and in the non-uniformity of action on the part of the government to deal with minority language rights issues from coast to coast. The government could do more, not less dismantling of social programs.
All of these factors contribute to the tensions that exist in our society. When these programs are not there, the very first to be excepted are the most vulnerable groups in our society, the new immigrants and the new citizens.
The underpinning, as has been said by my colleague, of any good programs and policies were they to succeed would be philosophy-the philosophy that we believe in individual freedom and initiative, that we believe in equality for all. But then, that principle without the concomitant principle of social conscience is not complete.
In conclusion, I would like to cite a description of discrimination given by Justice McIntyre of the Supreme Court of Canada. Justice McIntyre said:
Discrimination may be described as a distinction, whether intentional or not, but based on grounds relating to personal characteristics of the individual or group, which has the effect of imposing burdens, obligations, or disadvantages on such individuals or groups not imposed upon others, or which withholds or limits access to opportunities, benefits and advantages available to other members of society. Distinctions based on personal characteristics attributed to an individual solely on the basis of association with a group will rarely escape the charge of discrimination, while those based on an individual's merits and capabilities will rarely be so classed.
When we sincerely and seriously understand this message in our hearts and minds, then there will no longer be any need for this type of motion in the future. Today we remain challenged as Canadians to ensure that racial harmony prevails.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud and honoured to stand in this House today to discuss the motion put forward by the New Democratic Party.
I would like to share 10 minutes with my colleague from Delta.

Mr. Speaker, I would like today to share with the House my thoughts on a minority that is a very small but very significant percentage of the Canadian population and by that mean natives and the issue of native inmates.
Although natives account for 2,5 per cent of the Canadian population only their proportion is much higher in our inmate population, especially in the Prairies. They come from various language and cultural groups; some are status Indians, others are not. They include North-American Indians, Inuit and Metis. The native culture of course has its very own values and tenets. By reasons of those values and tenets, native
February 13, 1990

inmates have little understanding or interest for Correctional Services Canada's programs and services.
However, they participate fully in those activities that are organized by other natives or filled with native culture.
Native inmates account for some 10 per cent of the total inmate population. In some Prairie institutions, their proportion nears 50 per cent. They are not a homogeneous group, in the sense that they come from a variety of language and cultural nationalities within Canada's native population. As inmates, they do not participate in mainstream programs and services as much as non-native inmates, which restricts their eligibility for early parole. They are however attracted to activities in which other natives take part, that are introduced by natives or that have a native cultural content.
Generally, native inmates come from socially and economically under privileged communities. Drug and alcohol abuse often is a problem and seems to be a significant factor in offences, involving violence which are more common among natives than non-natives. Poor community conditions also make it difficult for native inmates to develop plans that would allow parole.
Native inmates have special needs and programs should respond to those needs. Although there is no national program that specifically addresses their culture, the Correctional Services have chosen the objective of providing services geared to their native inmates.
The Correctional Services' objective is to offer to native inmates programs and services that conform to their cultural and spiritual needs, in order that they may derive maximum benefit from the correctional process.
On February 15, 1989, my colleague the Solicitor General of Canada approved the Correctional Services' mandate. Strategic objective no 2.2 in the mandate includes the duty to:
Ensure that the special needs of native offenders be met -
Native spiritual programs have been developed since 1972 and are now available in most federal correctional institutions throughout the country.
Supply
The commissioner established a native advisory committee in 1974 to pave the way for discussions on correctional issues concerning native people. More specifically, the terms of reference of the committee include sharing information about native offenders and providing advice on matters related to the services available to and correctional programs for native people.
The committee is made up of Correctional Service Canada staff and representatives of major organizations which are responsible for keeping in touch with the native community and providing spiritual services to native offenders.
Correctional Service Canada officials consulted with spokesmen for the native people to set up programs and services to meet the needs of native inmates. This is why native liaison officers have been appointed in most institutions. They make sure that individual cases are handled in keeping with the cultural aspirations of native inmates so they will have ready access to treatment and social development activities tailored to their cultural background.
Native Elders also go to the institutions to offer spiritual guidance and officiate at sacred rites. Various other activities specifically intended for native people have also been planned in institutions where these people make up a high percentage of the inmate population.
Among such activities I might mention counselling by Elders, reading and writing lessons given by monitors, the temperance groups of the Sacred Circle, programs for re-integration in active life, drug addiction programs, traditional craft, and cultural events. Native fraternities or sororities organized and administered by native inmates operate in many correctional institutions. These group meet regularly, sometimes in the presence of a liaison officer and an Elder, to hold discussions, engage in cultural activities and attend ceremonies.
At the present time the wardens of institutions housing native inmates must make sure that, within the limits of institution security and order, religious programs are made available to the native people. They must see to it that such programs are consistent with native customs, including those which call for the use of traditional objects.

February 13, 1990
Supply
Correctional Service Canada provides services and programs for native offenders like Elders spiritual services. Elders perform traditional religious ceremonies, such as the pipe-smoking and fasting rituals, and act as spiritual advisors throughout the country.
In addition, the native liaison officers program has been extended. Under this program, native officers help native offenders prepare a discharge plan and establish contacts in the community. Special detoxification programs have been put in place and cultural activities have been organized in several places.
Halfway houses for natives, managed by native agencies and subsidized by Correctional Service Canada, offer post-release case management and support services in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Nova Scotia.
Academic upgrading programs for natives have been put in place in our penitentiaries. Native instructors prepare native inmates for life on the outside and give academic upgrading classes.
Making staff more sensitive to natives allows them to become familiar with their culture and more aware of their needs.
Native private agencies have been contracted by Correctional Service Canada to supervise native parolees. In some cases, community discharge programs for native inmates have been made possible by residential and parole supervision services provided by natives.
A training program in native values is offered to Correctional Service employees throughout the country, regionally or locally. There are native friendship groups supported by native liaison officers or elders. These self-help groups stress social, recreational, cultural and spiritual activities in institutions, or most institutions.
Corrections Canada offers a training program in traditional or contemporary native arts and crafts, drummaking and native traditions.
Mr. Speaker, I would have a lot to say and I have a great deal of pleasure in talking about minorities in our Canadian prisons or penitentiaries, for, as my colleague was just saying, everything is difficult for an immigrant, but I think that this government and the minister have
done much in the last five years, making the task easier and more culturally feasible.
In conclusion, this government and Corrections Canada work continuously with community interest groups to ensure that native offenders have programs and services that meet their cultural and spiritual needs.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I would just like to make a personal statement. If we go back 30 years when we became Canadians, you and I, and compare the hell then to the heaven now, as I was just saying, it is a privilege for everyone in Canada to be known as Canadians.

As the hon. member knows, family reunification is a fundamental basis of our immigration policy. For that we can all be proud. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity this afternoon of taking part in this veiy significant debate. It is unfortunate that the debate is in such a negative tone. I think that we in Canada have made real progress in the last few years in our racial relations. I say that coming from the west coast where we have had in the past very severe problems with our native Indians, the Chinese, the Japanese and the East Indians. I think matters have improved considerably, something which has been largely due to the policies of this government. However, we recognize that in Canada we still have significant problems with prejudices against minorities, whether they be racial, religious or whatever.
I would like to spend the few minutes that I have this afternoon to comment on the relationship with our native minorities. I believe that we just need to look at the Manitoba justice inquiry and also the Marshall inquiry to recognize that natives all over the country do suffer from the effects of ignorance and misunderstanding on the part of many Canadians.
Supply
We need to recognize also that these prejudices are rooted in hundreds of years of history and that to expect legislation to remove them in very short order is unrealistic. I think that it is worth while to look at some of the things that this government is doing and has done to correct that situation. We recognize that many of the problems that natives face are as a result of poverty and other social problems which our native population has to struggle against. Much needs to be done, both for our native Indians and also the Inuit.
I recognize that both of these groups of people have real hopes and ambitions just as the rest of Canadians have. The Ministers of Indian Affairs over the years have made many changes and changes will continue to be made as policies are required.
One of the major government policies that we are working on at the present time to allow the Indian population to take its rightful place in Canadian society is the promotion of self-government. We have seen, particularly in the last 10 to 15 years, the growing responsibility of the First Nations to assume responsibility for their educational, judicial, social and economic life.
Many of the disadvantages such as poverty are diminishing. As self-reliance and independence become the norm for our native people and the Inuit of Canada, Canadians are seeing the emergence of strong, dynamic partners in our economy, our cultural diversity and prosperity. Much evidence of our efforts to assist the native people can be seen and is becoming more obvious each year.
For example, there is the native justice system. As I mentioned earlier, this is a question which preoccupies all of us in the light of recent events in Canada. There was a federal task force conducted just recently on the question of reserve policing services. It has been shown that native communities are better served by law enforcement based on an understanding of the traditions and culture of these communities.
Administering the law at any time is not easy. It is important that those who are administering the law understand the cultural background of the people they are assisting.
Traditional Indian ways and practices increasingly enhance the peace and the harmony in our native communities. It is the goal of this government to

February 13, 1990
Adjournment Debate
enhance and increase the representation of native Canadians in the judicial system, as well as in the policing and legal professions. We have an example of that in our own party here in the House.
In many places in the country the number of native Indians in the prison population is entirely disproportionate to the general population. This would indicate to us very clearly that something is indeed wrong. Yet Canadians as a whole are developing a much greater awareness of the problems which our native Indians face.
Just last September there was an Angus Reid poll conducted in Canada. More than half of those polled believe native people were not treated fairly by the courts; and 70 per cent believe that native people have more difficulty getting hired for good jobs than do white Canadians. Most feel that aboriginal people deserve to be a lot better off financially than they are. It was not natives who said that but a cross-section of all Canadians.
Canadians in this same poll also said they are much more likely to support rather than to oppose aboriginal self-government. Over half of those surveyed agreed with the statement that the Canadian Constitution should specifically recognize the right of Indians to govern themselves on their own lands without interference from white society.
These are very encouraging opinions. We need to recognize that in spite of all the bad stories, there is a large reservoir of goodwill and understanding out there. These are the types of things we need to work with to culture and develop.
There have been many policies put out by Indian Affairs to do this in working with the native organizations. This bodes well for our growth as a tolerant and caring society.
I would like to thank the hon. member for Windsor- St. Clair for giving us this opportunity today to confront the fact of racism and bigotry in Canada and to consider our response as individuals, as members of Parliament and to renew our resolve as good men and women to do something about it. We know we must continue to ensure that the government carries out its duty to continue a relentless effort to eliminate racism and bigotry wherever it arises.

Mr. Speaker, on October 23,1 asked the Minister of Agriculture to stand up for the Canadian farmer rather than continue to stand idly by as the United States Secretary of Agriculture fulfilled his words with additional disciplinary action being taken in the area of Canadian farm subsidies.
At that time I pointed out that the government had already allowed the United States to discipline our pork industry and our milk producers and that it appeared that the United States wanted to discipline our Canadian Durum wheat producers. Although the Durum wheat producers had not yet been disciplined at that point, they were sending shipments of Durum wheat into the United States.
I note that at the present time they are not permitted to compete with the United States in that market as permits for export are no longer being issued by the Canadian Wheat Board. When the United States threatens to discipline us, the Canadian government does it for it by refusing to issue those permits.
The minister talked tough on that day, as he did recently in Toronto, but little or no action has been taken since that day in October.
In Toronto he said he might test Article 701.4 of the free trade agreement to see if it has any teeth. Clearly, as those in the fisheries know, the free trade agreement is all bark and no bite. If the free trade agreement had any bite, surely the government would have used it long ago.
On October 23,1 asked the minister to start disciplining the United States for its use of the Export Enhancement Program. The minister told Canadians on December 20, 1989, that the Bush administration wants to ratchet down export enhancement. The budget for the
February 13, 1990

Export Enhancement Program is $566 million U.S. for the year 1990. For 1991, the budget has been ratcheted up, rather than down, to $900 million.
On October 23, the minister dismissed the Durum farmers' concerns saying: "It demonstrates to the people of Canada and the world that Canada can compete with the best of them".
How is the Canadian farmer to compete with a $900 million United States subsidy that is stealing their markets away? How is the Canadian farmer to compete against American subsidies that Mr. Yeutter admits run at a level of $21,000 U.S. per farmer, $5,000 more than Canadians receive?
The minister told the House on October 23 that United States Durum producers receive subsidies of $40 to $50 a tonne more than Canadian producers of Durum wheat.
In the week of September 21 the United States sold 22,000 tonnes of Durum wheat under the Export Enhancement Program at a subsidized rate of $6.48 a tonne.
In October the United States sold hundreds of thousands of tonnes of grain to Egypt, Algeria and the USSR under an Export Enhancement Program of $8 a tonne.
On January 8, 1990, the United States sold 300,000 tonnes of grain to China under the Export Enhancement Program; and on January 10 it followed with a sale of up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat to Russia, subsidized at a rate of $20.50 a tonne, or 56 cents a bushel.
Now the minister is having a study done to determine the level of subsidies to United States farmers. Well, we on this side of the House have called on him to do that for almost a year. Has the minister looked into those subsidies? Can the minister not see the effects of the Export Enhancement Program? Perhaps he should read the farm income levels that his office issued in December.
What is our government doing to defend our farmers? What bold initiatives has the government undertaken to secure our world markets to ensure the viability of our farmers? The government cancelled $399 million worth
Adjournment Debate
of agriculture programs in the last budget so that it can claim to be the Boy Scouts of international trade.
Mr. Yeutter told the United States Senate in April of last year that "if the Geneva negotiations are successful, we will be writing a segment of the European communities 1991 farm bill in Geneva rather than Brussels. That is obviously one of our objectives. We will also be writing a major segment of the farm bills of Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Australia and seven other countries in Geneva and we want to do that too".
If we look at our budget in Canada in the 1989 period, and he did just that, the budget added $60 million a year to farm costs, and increased the costs of the average prairie farmer by $1,000 per year. How is the Canadian farmer is to compete with the $900 million United States export enhancement program?
The list of items cancelled in the last budget is incredible in the face of the escalating trade war. Crop insurance was cut by $200 million, the at and east grain and flour subsidy was cut by $60 million, the rail branch line rehabilitation program was cut by $48 million, grain and crop advance payments were cut by $54 million, the dairy export was cut by $12 million, commodity-based loans were cut by $15 million and the Canadian Dairy Commission was cut by $10 million. There were total cuts of $399 million.
I ask the government what it intends to do to counter the Export Enhancement Program while there still is an agricultural industry left in Canada, based on the concept of the family farm that has served us so well for so many years in this nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has put on the floor of the House a technical and complex question, and I will attempt to respond on behalf of the minister in those terms.
American Durum growers are wrong to complain continually about our exports of Durum for pasta and noodles, and they are wrong to threaten countervail action. American millers buy Canadian Durum because of Canadian quality and Canadian reliability. The U.S. Durum wheat industry and elected officials from North Dakota have alleged that prices for U.S. Durum have declined because of these imports. These concerns are not well founded.

February 13, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Canadian Durum sales have developed since late 1986 to supply growing U.S. demand for high-quality Durum wheat which U.S. growers are unable to meet because of short-falls of U.S. supplies. U.S. farmers reseeded a reduced acreage to Durum in 1988 which happened to coincide with drought-reduced yields 40 per cent below
1987	levels and more than 50 per cent below yields earlier in the decade.
The result of the reduced acreage, plus the reduced yield experienced in 1988, was that U.S. production declined by more than 50 per cent from the previous year to 45 million bushels, while the total supply declined by 28 per cent to 141 million bushels.
At the same time, domestic consumption increased sharply from 50 million bushels to 61 million bushels. In other words, production was not even sufficient to cover domestic needs. Even though U.S. exports declined from 62 to 20 million bushels, U.S. stocks had to be drawn down from 80 to 60 million bushels to make up for the production shortfall. Imports increased to 13 million bushels from 7 million the previous year in response to the drought-reduced supply.
U.S. stocks have dropped steadily despite marginal imports of Durum. Also, exports including subsidized exports of U.S. Durum have on average exceeded total domestic value. It should be noted that the U.S. subsidized the export of 7.3 million bushels of Durum exports at a total cost of U.S. $4.1 million to Algeria in 1988-89. This Durum was delivered during the period November
1988	to April 1989 when it was clearly apparent that U.S. production was insufficient to cover even domestic consumption.
Apparently production in 1988 returned to predrought levels and USDA forecasts that imports will decline by almost 25 per cent to 10 million bushels. Domestic consumption is expected to decline from earlier levels but still exceed pre-drought levels. Export levels are also expected to be near pre-drought levels. Our exports of Durum to the United States are normal commercial sales by the Canadian Wheat Board. There is no intention to artificially limit these sales, particularly when there is continuing demand for high-quality Durum.
Therefore, there is this explanation of the existing import-export. The suggestion the minister wants to make is that before U.S. authorities continue to make unsubstantiated claims that our exports are the cause of price declines in Durum that they take another look at what is going on within their own borders, and more specifically at their Export Enhancement Program. There is action today in the United States and our government welcomes the investigations which we are confident will show that any problem faced by U.S. Durum wheat producers are not caused by Canada.
