Mr. Speaker, when I asked a question of the Minister of National Defence on November 28, my question to him concerned the low-level flight training in Nitassinan. I asked if the minister would consider responding to these confidence building measures and peace moves by the Warsaw bloc to the Canadian women's groups, native groups, church and other groups which today were present in his office by restricting the low level flights and other training over Goose Bay and Nitassinan instead of increasing them from 7,000 to 40,000 according to the outdated NATO plan. Those are excerpts from my question.
His answer was:
The hon. member puts forward a suggestion that would mean that Canada would act unilaterally as a member of NATO.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, it would not be unilateral. Poland and other members of the Warsaw Pact had already been reducing their low level flights, and for Canada to respond would have been a bilateral response. So the minister's response was patently false. Therefore, there is a need to look at what is the basis of his answer. That is to say the basis of his answer is clearly suggested in the news release of October 31 which states:
The environmental impact statement concludes that increased low-level flight training and a NATO Centre hold the potential to secure the future of CFB Goose Bay and bring up to two billion dollars in economic and employment opportunities to Labrador, Newfoundland, and the rest of Canada.
In other words, the falsity of the minister's answer was clearly related to the claim of $2 billion potential benefit made in the environmental impact statement put out on behalf of the Department of National Defence.
February 13, 1990

This statement has been attacked by several dozen experienced and expert researchers on the environment, one of whom, a Dr. Bargen stated that he had examined about 150 pounds of such statements and this was the worst one that he has seen.
One thing they have done is to ignore the human problems that are now being caused by these flights. I refer to the study done by the experts hired by the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office from which I quote some of their remarks as reflected in today's The Globe and Mail:
High rates of alcoholism, suicides and teen-age pregnancies in the Goose Bay area of Labrador were ignored in an environmental impact study of the low-level flying done for the Department of National Defence, groups, representing doctors, lawyers and women say.
These are based on the study itself and on their critique of the study.
Marion Reran, spokesman for the Canadian Voice of Women for Peace, said the study has failed to examine the effect on native women of the proposed influx of 60,000 military personnel, most of them young men, if a North Atlantic Treaty Organization base for tactical low-level flying is established at Goose Bay.
She is quoted as saying:
There is no mention of the increase in alcoholism, sexually transmitted diseases, illegitimate babies, the housing crisis, social disruption and other issues pertinent to women and communities.
Another commentator, Marion Mathieson, spokesman for the National Action Committee of the Status of Women, said there is evidence of women living near military bases in Cold Lake, Alberta, West Germany and the Philippines being victims of sexual assault and suffering sexually transmitted diseases after contact with military men.
She went on to say that the consultants who drew up the impact-and this is quite serious, Mr. Speaker-study also ignored federal regulations requiring them to examine any impacts of a project because of the age or sex of the people affected. In other words, they did not look at the special effects of noise on children, and they did not look at the special effects of those military men, 60,000 of them, on the women of the neighbourhood.
The study was also attacked by Health Professionals for the Prevention of Nuclear War who stated that "the over-all scientific quality of the information presented is
Adjournment Debate
poor and the amount of information relating to health issues insufficient to support meaningful discussion."
The government hired three reviewers to look at this statement and one of them, Sheila Zurbrigg, said that it is unconscionable that the review did not examine predictions of increases in sexually transmitted diseases because of the increase in military personnel at the base.
Another matter that was improperly done was the study of the noise effects that the low-level flights would have. The study claimed that they would be negligible, but Doctor Zurbrigg said that the study did not examine the West German studies and the one done by the Canadian Public Health Association in 1987 which suggested that loud unexpected noise could cause physical and psychological problems, particularly for young people.
It is also pointed out by the Halifax chapter of the Lawyers for Social Responsibility that the study made a fundamental error in ignoring the land claims of both the native Innu and Inuit groups in Labrador. Both of these groups oppose the low-level flying because it disturbs the game on which they depend for hunting.
There are a number of other faults as well which are pointed out by an independent group of experts that reported yesterday. For example, they point out that the EIS from the Department of National Defence fails to properly assess the economic and social costs of the project. In fact, they say it is grossly inadequate in its assessment of the economic benefits. In other words, the $2 billion, according to these experts, ain't there. The $2 billion, which is obviously the motivation, is an exaggeration, not to mention the social costs.
They also point out that there is failure to include a specific plan. They talk about monitoring. They say that monitoring will fix it all up. They will monitor where the flights go and make sure there is nobody there, but they do not give any monitoring plan. The Innu have told us that in fact even when they have given them the co-ordinates and say they are going to be camping next week in such and such an area, the flights continue to over-fly them.

February 13, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Finally, there is inadequate assessment of past, present and future impacts of fuel dumping. Fuel is dumped in the rivers and lakes and has a poisonous effect on the fish.
All in all, the study has about 100 major flaws according to these experts. Yet today the government refused to give any serious response to the questions of the hon. member for Skeena as to whether that faulty, entirely inadequate study is going to be used as the excuse to go ahead, notwithstanding the severe environmental impacts.
I call on the Government to reconsider the whole environmental study, to start a new one and in the meantime, as the Innu had asked, to stop the low-level flight training until that new study has been completed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to make a preliminary remark to my colleague. In my answer, I will deal mostly with the first part of the question raised by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), in which he had asked supplementary questions. After that, I will be pleased to come back to the question of low-level flights, like he just mentioned, to give a more complete answer.

Even with the normalization of political and military relations in Europe, Canada will continue to require a modern, capable armed forces for air defence, for the defence of Canadian territory, for the defence of Canadian maritime interests and for participation in peacekeeping operations.
The hon. member will recognize that the changes that are taking place in Europe have the potential for changing not only the military threat in Europe, but the whole spectrum in east/west military balance.
As the Prime Minister has already stated to the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party, progress has been made in the last number of years and it has been remarkable in the last few months. Indeed, this progress has been brought about in large measure by the solidarity of NATO, and we propose to keep it that way.
Given the enormous changes that are taking place in eastern Europe on an almost daily basis, any changes to the current structure of the alliances could be destabilizing with respect to the initiatives that are currently under way.
The hon. member will recognize that we have made a series of recommendations for building bridges of friendship, including programs of talks and expanded military contact which reflects the dramatic improvement in east/west relations and contributes to the process of confidence-building in military affairs.
The hon. member will recall that in recent months, members of the Canadian Forces held meetings with their counterparts in the Soviet Union. Let me emphasize that their goal was that of confidence-building, of reaching understandings with one another and being able to bring about a climate of peace and security to the world. Flowever, Mr. Speaker, differences that are recognized by both sides remain and we should continue to be prudent. We consider that a cohesive and strong NATO alliance remains vital for both political and military consultation and for managing the transformation of east/west relations.

Mr. Speaker, the question which I raised had to do with the very serious problems which are affecting Atlantic Canada around the reduction of activities of National Sea Products. In the questions that I raised, I was particularly concerned with the results for the community of Canso and for the workers of National Sea within that community. There were essentially three questions which I raised.
The first question was to ask the government what it was planning to do for the future of those workers who would not benefit from jobs under the so-called saviour plan of National Sea. There was no answer to that question.
The second question was why the trade union involved representing those workers had been left out of the negotiations which had taken place. If those workers had been represented and able to put their point of view in the negotiation process, I would have thought that a much better result could have been expected. But they
February 13, 1990

were not represented. I raised the question, and once more no answer was given by the government.
Finally, I asked the government when it was going to protect workers in Atlantic Canada-and one could make the same point for workers across the country- from arbitrary plant shutdowns on the part of companies that do not take into account the serious detrimental impact on local communities which results. To that as well there was no answer provided.
The reality which results for the community of Canso, for the plant operations in that community, can be summarized in the following terms: the trawler fleet itself of National Sea has been taken out of the community, 120 jobs permanently lost; the marine division, 70 jobs permanently lost; the outside wharf work, 100 jobs permanently lost; the night shift, 175 jobs permanently lost; the meal plant, 50 jobs permanently lost.
Employees will not be entitled to severance pay because the company does not consider this a plant closure. When the plant reopens, a maximum of 150 jobs will be provided in a plant where 750 people once worked. It is true that these jobs will be shared so that there might be perhaps 300 people who benefit from the jobs themselves and the UI benefits which result from them, but there will only be 150 jobs left and fish will be trucked into Canso from other National Sea facilities in Lunenburg or Louisburg.
There is no guarantee of how much work per year will be available. For the community, this will be devastating with 600 people no longer earning an income. The result, as the union put it this proposed saviour plan, is nothing more than a band-aid resolve to a situation which required major surgery. The life of this community will be slowly sucked out.
I come from the community of Windsor, Ontario, in which the same kind of detrimental impact hit our major employer, Chrysler, in the early 1980s. The government of this country provided help. As a result of that help Chrysler revived and now provides tremendous employment possibilities throughout the community.
The community of Canso and the Atlantic fisheries communities in general deserve the same kind of generous response from the Government of Canada. It is with great disappointment that I see this government's failure
Adjournment Debate
to provide that kind of generosity and care for the people of the communities of Atlantic Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by reminding the hon. member for Essex-Windsor it was National Sea that made the decision to close the fish plant in the town of Canso.
It was when the Government of Canada and the Province of Nova Scotia prevailed upon National Sea Products to review their decision that the board of directors of the company met on February 6 to approve a plan which was intended to help safeguard the future of the town of Canso.
National Sea Products Canso plant and trawler port were scheduled to close permanently on April 2, because the company did not have enough fish to process, having lost 159 million pounds of fish quota since 1984.1 do not have to remind the member of the difficulties, the crushing problems, that have been created by the depletion of the fish resource.
After extensive discussions with the Government of Nova Scotia and the federal government, the company decided that the plant in the town of Canso would remain open and would provide 300 time shared jobs on a long-term basis. The trawler port of Canso will close as scheduled on April 2, 1990. However, subject to the collective agreements in place at other National Sea trawler ports, the company expects the 128 trawlermen employed at Canso to have employment opportunities at those other ports.
This decision is made possible by National Sea's increased processing of fish from the pool of underutilized species, as identified by the federal government in the 1990 groundfish management plan and utilization of other fish available to the company in 1991.
In addition, the company has made application under generally available programs from federal and provincial government funding to replace the plant's refrigeration system for environmental reasons. The plant is expected to close as scheduled on April 2 to begin the replacement of the refrigeration system which will allow for the projected future work. Because of the environmental sensitivity and scope of the project, the plant is expected to reopen by December 1990.

February 13, 1990
Adjournment Debate
I want to assure the member that the Government of Canada, the Minister of Public Works and the ministry generally are working with ACOA, National Sea Products and the Government of Nova Scotia to provide whatever assistance can be made available so that this package will be provided to the company in order to keep the Canso plant open indefinitely.
At the same time, I want to respond to one or more other comments that the member made, because he should know that other programs will be made available to workers. The Older Workers Program will be one of those that can be applied in this case. He mentioned the involvement of the trade union and the workers of the plant. Of course, the Minister of Public Works and the government are well aware of the role played by workers. Indeed the whole purpose of the exercise is to ensure that whatever work can be made available to the workers is made available.
I hope the hon. member and the people of Canso will not take the attitude taken by Mr. Jim Sorrell of the
Canadian Auto Workers, as reported in the February 7 issue of the Halifax Chronicle Herald, because he said that "the town is history" according to that media report.
We are all trying with all the resources at our disposal to ensure that the plant is kept open and that there is as much work as possible for the plant workers and the trawlermen. In that way we hope to preserve the town of Canso.
